For fixed $\alpha>-1/2$, $\beta>-1/2$, $\alpha+\beta>1$: $\int_1^T\zeta^{(\mu)}(\alpha+ti)\zeta^{(\nu)}(\beta-ti)dt\sim\ldots T$ (Hadamard, Landau, Schnee), the case $\mu=\nu=0$, $\alpha=\beta=\sigma>1/2$ giving $\int|\zeta(\sigma+it)|^2\sim\zeta(2\sigma)T$.

As $t\to\infty$: $\zeta^2(\tfrac12+it)=\sum_{n\le t/2\pi}d(n)n^{-1/2-it}+\big(\tfrac{t}{2\pi}\big)^{-2it}\!\!\cdots\sum d(n)n^{-1/2+it}+O(\log t)$, i.e. $\zeta^2=S+\bar{\bar{S}}$-type main sum $\sum_{n\le t/2\pi}d(n)n^{-1/2-it}$ plus a twisted conjugate sum $+O(\log t)$ (communicated to Ingham by Hardy and Littlewood; proof not published at the time).
role: Replaces the usual AFE in Theorem B; the main term from diagonal $m=n$ gives $(1/4)T\log^4T\cdot$... resulting in $\frac{1}{2\pi^2}T\log^4T$.

statement: As $x\to\infty$: $\sum_{n\le x}\frac{d(n)^2}{n}=\frac1{4\pi^2}\log^4x+O(\log^3x)$ (via Ramanujan's formula $\sum_{n\le x}d(n)^2=\frac1{\pi^2}x\log^3x+O(x\log^2x)$).
role: Gives the diagonal term of the mean fourth power: $\frac1{2\pi^2}T\log^4T$.
location: Section 6, p. 296; Landau Hilfssatz 10, Hardy-Littlewood Lemma 3.51 cited

statement: Landau/Hardy-Littlewood-type bounds for the off-diagonal sums $\sum_{m\ne n}\frac{d(m)d(n)}{\sqrt{mn}\,|\log(m/n)|}=O(T\log^3T)$ [with the cutoff $m,n\le T'/2\pi$] and its oscillatory counterpart $O(\sqrt T\log^3T)$.
role: Control of the non-diagonal terms in $\int|S|^2dt$.

statement: For complex $s$: $\zeta(s)=\frac{\Gamma(1-s)}{2\pi i}\cdot(\text{Hankel contour integral }\int_{C(0)}\frac{z^{-s}}{e^{-z}-1}dz)$-type variant of Riemann's contour formula; splitting with parameters $x,y$ gives $\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\le x}n^{-s}+\chi(s)\sum_{n\le y}n^{s-1}+\Omega(x,y,s)$ and $\chi(s)\chi(1-s)=1$, $\Omega(x,y,s)=\chi(s)\Omega(y,x,1-s)$ (eq. (20)-(22)).
role: Starting point of the proof of Theorem A: a variant of the approximate functional equation with an explicit remainder Omega treated directly (not merely by inequality), which is what eliminates Littlewood's extra error term.

statement: Let $K\subset D(1/2,1)=\{1/2<\sigma<1\}$ be compact with connected complement and $f\in H_0^c(K)$ (continuous on $K$, holomorphic in the interior, non-vanishing on $K$). Then for every $\varepsilon>0$, $\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\,\mathrm{meas}\{\tau\in[0,T]:\sup_{s\in K}|\zeta(s+i\tau)-f(s)|<\varepsilon\}>0$.
hypotheses: K compact in the open strip 1/2<Re s<1, connected complement
f continuous, holomorphic inside, zero-free on K

statement: Let $\varphi(s)=\sum a(n)n^{-s}$ lie in the Selberg class with degree $d_\varphi$, $\sigma_\varphi=\max\{1/2,1-d_\varphi^{-1}\}$, and suppose $\sum_{p\le x}|a(p)|^2=(\lambda+o(1))x/\log x$ for some $\lambda>0$. Then $\varphi$ is universal in $D(\sigma_\varphi,1)$.

For normalized Hecke eigen cusp forms $g,g_1,g_2$: (i) $\zeta,L(s,g)$ jointly universal in $D(1/2,1)$; (ii) $L(s,g_1),L(s,g_2)$ jointly universal in $D(1/2,1)$ if $g_1\ne g_2$; (iii) $\zeta, L(s,\mathrm{sym}^2 g)$ in $D(2/3,1)$; (iv) $\zeta, L(s,g_1\otimes g_2)$ in $D(3/4,1)$ for $g_1\neq g_2$; (v) $L(s,g_1), L(s,g_1\otimes g_2)$ in $D(3/4,1)$.
If $\varphi$ is strongly universal in $D(a,b)$ (universality for all $f\in H^c(K)$, zeros allowed), then there is $C>0$ with $N(T;\sigma_1,\sigma_2;\varphi)\ge CT$ for all $a<\sigma_1<\sigma_2<b$.
location: Sec. 5, (5.3); proof with f(s)=s-sigma_0 on a disc

statement: $\zeta$ is not strongly universal in $D(1/2,1)$, since $N(T;\sigma_1,\sigma_2;\zeta)=o(T)$ for $1/2<\sigma_1<\sigma_2<1$ (zero-density estimates).

RH for $\zeta$ holds iff for every compact $K\subset D(1/2,1)$ with connected complement and every $\varepsilon>0$, $\liminf_T \frac1T\mathrm{meas}\{\tau\in[0,T]:\sup_{s\in K}|\zeta(s+i\tau)-\zeta(s)|<\varepsilon\}>0$ (strong recurrence, (9.1)). Extended to Dirichlet L-functions (Bagchi) and Beurling zeta functions (R. Steuding).

For $d$ irrational, or $d=a/b$ non-zero rational with $(a,b)=1$ and $|a-b|\ne1$: $\liminf_T\frac1T\mathrm{meas}\{\tau\le T:\sup_K|\zeta(s+i\tau)-\zeta(s+id\tau)|<\varepsilon\}>0$ (9.3). The log version (9.4) holds for every $d\ne0$; (9.3) at $d=0$ is the RH-equivalent (9.1), and (9.4) at $d=0$ would imply RH.

For $0<\varepsilon\le1/2$, $f\in H(K(0.05))$ with $\max_{K(0.06)}|f|\le1$: $d(\log\zeta,f,K(0.0001),\varepsilon)\ge\exp(-\varepsilon^{-13})$ and $\tau(\log\zeta,f,K(0.0001),\varepsilon)\le\exp\exp(10\varepsilon^{-13})$.

If $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$, then for any $\theta_k$ and $\varepsilon>0$, $\lim_T\frac1T\mathrm{meas}\{\tau\le T:\|\tau\alpha_k-\theta_k\|<\varepsilon\ \forall k\}>0$.
role: Applied to $\alpha_p=\log p/2\pi$ to realize arbitrary phases of finitely many Euler factors.

statement: Every $f\in H^c(K)$, $K$ compact with connected complement, is a uniform limit of polynomials on $K$.
role: Used by Gonek and Bagchi to reduce arbitrary targets to polynomial/exponential targets.

statement: Replacing the Mertens-type asymptotic $\sum_{p\le x}|a(p)|^2/p=\log\log x+a_1+O(\cdot)$ by a PNT-type positive density $\sum_{p\le x}|\tilde a(p)|^2=(1+o(1))x/\log x$ suffices for Bagchi's argument.
role: Extends universality from $\zeta$ to cusp-form L-functions (Laurincikas-Matsumoto, Theorem 3), Selberg class (Thm 4).

statement: If $\sup_{|s-\sigma_0|\le\delta}|\varphi(s+i\tau)-(s-\sigma_0)|<\delta$, then $\varphi(\cdot+i\tau)$ has exactly one zero in $|s-\sigma_0|<\delta$.
role: Converts strong universality into a positive-density zero count off the critical line.

statement:
Let $F\in\widetilde{\mathcal S}^\#_1$ (extended Selberg class, degree 1) and $\alpha>0$. Then the linear twist $F(s,\alpha)=\sum a_F(n)n^{-s}e(-n\alpha)$ is entire if $a_F(n_\alpha)=0$ (with $n_\alpha=q_F\alpha$, and $a_F(n_\alpha):=0$ if $n_\alpha
otin\mathbb N$). If $a_F(n_\alpha)
eq0$ it has at most simple poles at $s_k=1- rac{k+i	heta_F}{1}$... i.e. $s_k=1-k-i	heta_F$, $k=0,1,\dots$, with residue at $s_0$ equal to $c(F)\,a_F(n_\alpha)/n_\alpha^{i	heta_F}$, $c(F)
eq0$.

For $d>0$, $F\in\widetilde{\mathcal S}$ of degree $d_F=d$ and $\alpha>0$, the non-linear twist $F_d(s,\alpha)=\sum a_F(n)n^{-s}e(-n^{1/d}\alpha)$ is entire if $a_F(n_\alpha)=0$, where $n_\alpha=q_F d^{-d}\alpha^d$; otherwise it has at most simple poles at $s_k=\frac{d+1}{2d}-\frac{k}{d}-i\frac{\theta_F}{d}$, $k=0,1,\dots$, with $c_0(F,\alpha)\neq0$ at $s_0$.
location: Sec. 5, p. 89 (the survey's own transcription of $n_\alpha$ and $s_k$ is partly garbled in the text layer, so exact constants should be checked against [29])

statement: For $1<d<2$, $F\in\widetilde{\mathcal S}^d$, $\alpha>0$, $J\ge1$: there are $c_0\neq0$ and polynomials $P_j(s)$ ($P_0=c_0$) such that for $\sigma^*>\sigma_a(F)$, $F(s,\alpha)=q_F^{ks}\sum_{j<J}\alpha^{k(d_Fs-d_F/2+i\theta_F+j)}P_j(s)D_F(s^*+jk,\alpha)+G_J(s,\alpha)$ with $G_J$ holomorphic for $\sigma^*>\sigma_a(F)-kJ$, $k=1/(d_F-1)$ (overconvergence).

(6.2) If $F\in\widetilde{\mathcal S}^\#_1$ then $q_F\in\mathbb N$, $a_F(n)n^{i\theta_F}$ is periodic mod $q_F$, $\eta_F\in\{-1,0\}$, and F is uniquely a sum over characters $\chi$ of $P_\chi(s+i\theta)L(s+i\theta,\chi^*)$ with Dirichlet polynomials $P_\chi$ of degree-0 type; $\dim_{\mathbb R}V^\#_1(q,\xi,\omega^*)$ is finite (explicit formula). (6.3) If $F\in\mathcal S_1$ (Selberg class) and $q_F=1$ then $F=\zeta$; if $q_F\ge2$ then $F(s)=L(s+i\theta_F,\chi)$ for a primitive character $\chi$ mod $q_F$ with $\chi(-1)=-(\eta_F+1)\cdot$(sign as stated).
hypotheses: Euler product and Ramanujan for S_1 in (6.3)

statement: $\widetilde{\mathcal S}^\#_d=\emptyset$ for $1<d<5/3$; moreover for $1<d<2$ no $F\in\widetilde{\mathcal S}^\#_d$ has a pole at $s=1$. Hence $\mathcal S_d=\emptyset$ for $0<d<1$ (Conrey-Ghosh, cited elsewhere), $\mathcal S_1\ni$ only zeta/Dirichlet, and no new degrees in $(1,5/3)$.
hypotheses: F in extended Selberg class with d in (1,5/3)

statement: Let $I$ be a continuous, additive, real-valued invariant of the (extended) Selberg class. Then either $I(\mathcal S)$ has Lebesgue measure 0 or $I(\mathcal S)-I(\mathcal S)=\mathbb R$. Same for the extended class.

label_in_source: Theorem 6.6 ([14], unpublished, proof given in survey)
statement: Assume every $F\in\mathcal S^\#_d$ with $d\in\mathbb N$ has a $\gamma$-factor with all $\lambda_j=\tfrac12$. Then the exceptional set $E=\{d>0: d\notin\mathbb N,\ \widetilde{\mathcal S}_d\ne\emptyset\}$ satisfies $E\cap\mathbb Q=\emptyset$ and $m(E)=0$.
hypotheses: as stated; proof via Molteni n-th-root criterion for gamma factors, multiplicative semigroup structure, Steinhaus-type sum-set theorem
conditional_on: integer-degree functions have all lambda_j=1/2 in a gamma-factor

statement: Under Hypothesis S ($\sum_{p\le x}a_i(p)\overline{a_j(p)}/p=\delta_{ij}n_j\log\log x+c_{ij}+O(1/\log x)$) and Hypothesis D (density estimate $N_j(\sigma,T)\ll T^{1-a(\sigma-1/2)}\log T$ uniformly for $\sigma\ge1/2$): the vector $(\log F_j(1/2+it)/\sqrt{\pi n_j\log\log t})_j$ has weak limit the standard Gaussian on $\mathbb C^N$ (Thm 7.2, Selberg/Bombieri-Hejhal), also in short intervals of length $\ge\log T/\log\log T$ type scale (7.3). Thm 7.4: for $F_j$ with a common functional equation, GRH and Hypothesis H0, all but $o(T\log T)$ zeros up to T of a linear combination $\sum c_jF_j$ are simple and on the critical line. Thm 7.7: distinct $F,G\in\mathcal S$ with $d_F=d_G$ satisfying S and D have $\Delta(T;F,G)\gg T\log T$ (non-effective constant).

7.5 ([38]): for distinct $F,G\in\mathcal S$, $\Delta(T;F,G)=\Omega(T)$ (unconditional). 7.6 ([52] Srinivas): distinct $F,G\in\mathcal S$ with $d_F=d_G$: for large T there is a zero $\rho$ of F with $m_F(\rho)>m_G(\rho)$ and $|T-\rho|\ll\log\log T$, hence $\Delta\gg T/\log\log T$. 7.8 ([25]): if $\log F_1,\dots,\log F_N$ are $\mathbb Q$-linearly independent and $H$ a nonconstant polynomial-type function in the class $\mathcal H$, then $h(s)=H(\log F_j)$ has infinitely many singularities in $\sigma>1/2$ (key Lemma 7.1: infinitely many N-tuples of zeros whose multiplicity vectors form a basis of $\mathbb R^N$). 7.10 ([39]): the pair correlation conjecture PC implies the simple-zeros and distinct-zeros conjectures 7.1, 7.2; if the PC asymptotic holds for some $\alpha_0>0$ then unique factorization follows.

For $1<d<2$ and $F\in\widetilde{\mathcal S}^d$, the Rankin-Selberg-type series $F\otimes\bar F(s)=\sum|a_F(n)|^2n^{-2s}$-type (6.2) is holomorphic for $\sigma>\sigma_a(F)-k$ except for a simple pole at $s=1$.
role: Used in Thm 6.4 to remove the Ramanujan axiom (iv) from the argument.

statement: If $\log F_1,\dots,\log F_N$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$ there are infinitely many N-tuples of zeros $(\rho_1,\dots,\rho_N)$ in $\sigma>1/2$ with multiplicity vectors $m(\rho_j)$ forming a basis of $\mathbb R^N$.
role: Engine of the functional independence Thm 7.8.

statement: For $d_F=1$ the Fox hypergeometric function $H_K(-iy,s)$ is holomorphic for $y\ne\beta$ and $H_K(-i\beta,s)$ has at most simple poles at $s_k=1-k-i\theta_F$, nonvanishing residue at $s_0$ (here $\beta=\prod\lambda_j^{-2\lambda_j}$).
role: Computes the polar structure of the linear twist from the functional equation via the Mellin-Barnes representation (5.2).

statement: $F_N(s,\alpha)=R_N(s,\alpha)+\omega Q^{1-2s}\sum a_F^-(n)\,H_K(Q^2n\zeta_N,s)$, from shifting the contour in $F_N(s,\alpha)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int F(s+w)\Gamma(w)\zeta_N^{-w}dw$, $\zeta_N=\frac1N-2\pi i\alpha$, then using the functional equation.
role: Starting identity for all twist results; N→∞ afterwards.

statement: Let I(T)=\int_0^T|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|^2dt. For T>\tau_0 and A T<N<A'T (any fixed 0<A<A'), I(T)=T\log T-T(1+\log 2\pi-2\gamma)+\Sigma_1+\Sigma_2+O(\log^2T) where, schematically, \Sigma_1 is a sum over n\le N of terms of size (T/2\pi)^{1/4}\sqrt2\,(-1)^n d(n)n^{-3/4}\,e(T,n)^{-1}\sin\big(2T\sinh^{-1}\sqrt{\pi n/2T}+\sqrt{2\pi nT+\pi^2n^2}-\pi/4\big)-type with e(T,n) =(1+\pi n/2T)^{1/4}-type amplitude, and \Sigma_2=-2\sum_{n\le N'}d(n)n^{-1/2}\big(\log\tfrac{T}{2\pi n}\big)^{-1}\sin\big(T\log\tfrac{T}{2\pi n}-T+\tfrac\pi4\big)-type, N'=\tfrac{T}{2\pi}+O(\sqrt T)-type cutoff. Exact amplitude/phase forms are taken from a garbled OCR of p.354 and from memory of the standard statement (E(T)=\Sigma_1+\Sigma_2+O(\log^2 T)); must be rechecked against the PDF image before citation. d(n) is the divisor function.
location: p. 354 (Theorem), assembled at the end (substituting (7.1),(7.2),(8.2),(10.2) into (4.4))

statement: For 0<\Re u<1: \zeta(u)\zeta(1-u)=\tfrac12\zeta(1-u)\Big[\tfrac{\Gamma'}{\Gamma}(1-u)+\tfrac{\Gamma'}{\Gamma}(u)\Big]\!\!\Big|_{\text{(schematic)}}+2\gamma-\log 2\pi+g(u,1-u)+g(1-u,u), with g(u,v)=2\sum_{n\ge1}d_{?}\ldots (see (3.2)); exact form garbled in OCR.
For \Re u,\Re v>1: \zeta(u)\zeta(v)=\zeta(u+v)+f(u,v)+f(v,u), where f(u,v)=\sum_{r\ge1}\sum_{s\ge1}r^{-u}(r+s)^{-v}; f is meromorphic for \Re(u+v)>0.
role: Reduces |zeta|^2 to a double series classified by m-n, enabling Poisson summation.

statement: For \Re u<0,\Re v>1,\Re(u+v)>0, g(u,v)=2\sum_{n\ge1}\sigma_{u+v-1}(n)\int_0^\infty y^{-u}(1+y)^{-v}\cos 2\pi ny\,dy-type, giving a divisor-sum expansion (g defined via f and Gamma factors as in (1.4)).
role: Produces a single series with divisor-type coefficients; analytic continuation to the critical line.

statement: Using Voronoi's formula d(n)=D(x)+\Delta(x) with \Delta(x) expressed by Bessel-type series (error O(x^{1/2}\log x)), g(u,1-u) is continued to \Re u=1/2 and I(T) is written as T\log T-T(1+\log2\pi-2\gamma)+I_1-I_2+I_3-I_4+O(1) (eq. (4.4)) with explicit oscillatory integrals (4.5),(4.6).
role: Core structural step: approximate-functional-equation-type expression integrated along the critical line.

statement: Saddle-point lemma for \int_a^b\phi(x)\exp\{2\pi i(f(x)+kx)\}dx with f real, f''>0 on [a,b], f,\phi analytic in strips |z-x|\le\mu(x) with bounds \phi=O(\Phi), f=O(F\mu^{-1}), (f')^{-1}=O(\mu^2\Phi^{-1}) (exact conditions garbled), giving main term at the stationary point x_0 of f'+k plus explicit endpoint and error terms.
role: General first-derivative saddle-point/stationary-phase tool used for every oscillatory integral.

statement: Asymptotic evaluation (stationary point plus O(a^{...}T^{-...})+O(b...)+R(T,k)) of integrals \int_a^b y^{-\alpha}(1+y)^{-\beta}(\log\tfrac{1+y}{y})^{-\gamma}\exp i\{T\log\tfrac{1+y}{y}+2\pi ky\}dy under a,b,\alpha,\beta,\gamma bounded etc. (statement garbled in OCR).
role: Application of Lemma 1 to the integral types in I_1,I_2,I_3,I_4.

statement: Evaluation of the I_4-type integral: for n with T/(\pi(n^2-n)^{...})-type condition (10.1) the integral equals a main term involving d(n)n^{-1/2}(\log(T/2\pi n))^{-1}\sin(T\log\tfrac{T}{2\pi n}-T+\tfrac\pi4) plus O(T^{-1/2}...) (garbled).
role: Produces the second group of oscillating terms, truncated at Z=T/2\pi+O(\sqrt T); tails controlled by partial summation with the divisor asymptotic.

statement: Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb C$ be an open disk or half-space. $u\in L^\infty(\partial\Omega)$ with $u\bar u=1$ is quasi-inner if $(1-P)uP$ is compact, $P$ the orthogonal projection of $L^2(\partial\Omega)$ onto the Hardy space $H^2(\Omega)$. Inner functions are quasi-inner; products of quasi-inner functions are quasi-inner; on the unit disk, $(1-P)uP\sim JH_u$ modulo finite rank where $H_u$ is the Hankel operator with symbol $u$.

$\rho_\infty(z)=\pi^{-z/2}\Gamma(z/2)/(\pi^{-(1-z)/2}\Gamma((1-z)/2))$ is quasi-inner relative to $C_-=\{\mathrm{Re}\,z\le\tfrac12\}$, and $(1-P)\rho_\infty P$ is an infinitesimal of infinite order. Theorem 2.3 gives explicit rank-one expansion $(1-P)\kappa P=\sum_n(-1)^{n+1}\frac{2\pi^{2n+1/2}}{(4n+1)\Gamma(n+1)\Gamma(n+1/2)}|\xi_n\rangle\langle\eta_n|$ for $\kappa=\rho_\infty\circ\psi$, $\psi(v)=\frac12+\frac{v-1}{v+1}$ (Cayley-type map). Proposition 2.4 independently: $\kappa\in C^\infty(S^1)+H^\infty(\mathbb U)$.

For a rational prime $p$, $\rho_p(z)=\frac{1-p^{z-1}}{1-p^{-z}}$ (as ratio of $\gamma_p$) is periodic of period $\log p$ with poles on $\frac{2\pi i}{\log p}\mathbb Z$ and is not quasi-inner (Fact 3.6). With $B_p$ the Blaschke product attached to its poles, $\kappa_pB_p=-p\frac{v+1}{v-1}$-type inner function (Prop 3.7(i)), $\ker(1-P)\kappa_pP$ is the shift-invariant subspace $B_pH^2(\mathbb U)$, and the cokernel is its image under the involution $Jf(z)=z^{-1}f(z^{-1})$.

For any finite set $F$ of places of $\mathbb Q$ containing $\infty$, $u=\rho_\infty\prod_{p\in F\setminus\{\infty\}}\rho_p$ is quasi-inner relative to $C_-$. For a single prime, $\rho_\infty\rho_p$ is quasi-inner and $(1-P)\kappa\kappa_pP=E_\infty+E_p+E_0$ (explicit sum over poles); for general $F$ (Thm 4.8, with $\rho_\infty=\prod_{k=0}^{m-1}\varphi_{m,k}$ via Gauss multiplication) $\rho_\infty^{(m,k)}\rho_p$ is quasi-inner and $(1-P)\rho_\infty\prod\rho_pP$ is an infinitesimal of order $\frac1{2m}$ (m=number of finite places-based factorization; stated as 'order 1/2m'). Each individual $\rho_p$ is not quasi-inner.
hypotheses: uses decay of rho_infty on the imaginary line (Lemma 4.3, Lemma 4.6)

statement: (i) For $F$ finite containing the archimedean place and $u(F)=\prod_F\rho_v$, the Sonin space $S(u(F))=\ker (u(F))_{22}$ is infinite dimensional. Prop 5.5: the image under $F_\mu\circ w$ of Sonin's space $S(1,1)$ equals $\ker(1-P)\rho_\infty(1-P)=\ker(\rho_\infty)_{22}$.

For finite sets $F\subset F'$ as above, multiplication by $D(F,F')=\prod_{p\in F'\setminus F}(1-p^{-z})$ defines an injective linear map $S(u(F))\to S(u(F'))$; hence the semi-local Sonin spaces form an inductive system of infinite dimensional spaces. Proof: $N_F=\prod(1-p^{z-1})\in H^\infty(C_-)$, $D_F=\prod(1-p^{-z})\in H^\infty(C_+)$ (Lemma 5.6), so $\xi\in S(u(F))$ implies $D\xi\in H^2(C_+)$ and $u(F')D\xi=N_{F''}u(F)\xi\in H^2(C_-)$.
hypotheses: F subset F' finite sets containing infinity

statement: $\rho_p$ is $\log p$-periodic; Lemma 3.2-3.4 give an explicit basis $\zeta_n\in\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ and an isomorphism $V:\ell^2(\mathbb Z)\to\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, $V(\delta_n)=\zeta_n$; Lemma 3.5 gives $(1-P)\kappa_pP$ in terms of $V$ and the involution $I(\delta_n)=\delta_{-n}$.
role: Computation of the off-diagonal block for a single prime.

statement: Estimates on the decay of $\rho_\infty$ (and of its Gauss-factor pieces $\rho_\infty^{(m,k)}$) on the imaginary line; the terms $|\rho_\infty^{(m,k)}(\frac{2\pi in}{\log p})|=O(n^{-1/(2m)})$.
role: Key analytic input for compactness of $(1-P)\rho_\infty\rho_pP$ and for the order of infinitesimal.

statement: $\kappa(v)\kappa_p(v)\in C(S^1)+H^\infty(\mathbb U)$ (in fact smooth away from $v=1$).
role: Alternative route to quasi-innerness (Hankel compactness via Hartman).

statement: For a triangular block matrix of operators $U$ (modulo compacts, quasi-inner), the structure of the unitary is governed by the kernel of the matrix element $U_{22}$.
role: Motivates defining the semi-local Sonin space as $\ker U_{22}$.

statement: Using the Gauss multiplication formula for $\Gamma$, $\rho_\infty=\prod_{k=0}^{m-1}\varphi_{m,k}$ with each factor quasi-inner and having the decay properties of $\rho_\infty$ so that the products $\varphi_{m,k}\rho_p$ remain quasi-inner for $m$ large relative to the number of primes.
role: The 'fundamental step' to pass from one prime to m primes.

statement: The scaling action of $\mathbb R_+^*$ on $L^2(\mathbb R)$ quantizes $H=PQ$ (with $x\partial_x+\frac12$ as unitary generator, $H=2\pi pq$ with the number-theoretic Fourier normalization); passing from the absorption spectrum of [10] to the emission spectrum of Berry-Keating does not introduce a semi-classical mismatch, the cutoff of Berry-Keating is equivalent semiclassically to removing the 'white light', and the minus sign survives in the Maslov phases (statement of aims in the Introduction; computations in Sect. 1 not verified here).

The trace of the scaling action on $L^2(X_S)$, $X_S=\mathbb A_S/\mathbb Q_S^*$, for a finite set $S\ni\infty$ of places of Q, is given by the local terms of the Riemann-Weil explicit formula (semi-local trace formula).
hypotheses: S finite containing the archimedean place
location: Introduction / Sect. 2.2, Lemma 2.4 (recalled, not read in detail)

statement: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space, $u$ unitary, $F=2P-1$ with $P$ an orthogonal projection, $d^-u=[F,u]$. The following are equivalent: (i) $Pu^*(1-P)uP=-\frac12u^{-1}d^-u$; (ii) $u^{-1}d^-u\le0$; (iii) $Pu=PuP$.
In the one-variable quantized calculus, the equivalent conditions of Lemma 3.4 hold iff $u^*$ is an inner function in the sense of Beurling.
hypotheses: u a unitary function on the circle/line, F as in Def 2.1

statement: At a prime $p$, $u_p(s)=\frac{1-p^{-(1-z)}}{1-p^{-z}}$, $z=\frac12+is$ (modulus 1 on the critical line) has poles at $z\in\frac{2\pi i}{\log p}\mathbb Z$ (so is meromorphic, not holomorphic, in the left half plane) and is unbounded on the right half plane ($\sim -p^{z-1}$ as $z\to\infty$ real). At the archimedean place $u_\infty(s)=\phi(\frac12+is)$, $\phi(z)=\frac{\pi^{-z/2}\Gamma(z/2)}{\pi^{-(1-z)/2}\Gamma((1-z)/2)}$, holomorphic in $\mathrm{Re}z\ge\frac12$ but unbounded there (e.g. $\phi(20)=\frac{1856156927625}{8\pi^{20}}\approx26.4562$). Hence no $u_v^*$ is inner and Li's direct approach cannot work.

The inequality (3.1), $\sum_{\mathbb Q_S^*}|1-w|\,h(w)\,d^*w\le0$-type semi-local positivity (here with $h=h_1\star h_2$, $h_2(w)=h_1(w^{-1})$) does not hold in general: for $S=\{\infty\}$ it would force $i u_\infty^{-1}u_\infty'$ to have constant sign, i.e. the Riemann-Siegel angle $\theta$ (where $u_\infty(s)=e^{2i\theta(s)}$) to be monotonic, which is false.
hypotheses: S reduced to the archimedean place
no support restriction on the test functions
location: Sect. 3, Fact 3.6 (eq 3.1 at line ~612 of extracted text)

statement: The semi-local operator theoretic framework with $S:=\{\infty\}\cup\{p\mid p<q\}$ suffices to prove the Weil inequality for all test functions with support in the interval $(q^{-1/2},q^{1/2})$, where Weil positivity is $h=h_1\star h_2$ with $h_1$ satisfying the two conditions $\int_0^\infty h_1(x)x^{\pm1/2}d^*x=0$ (eq. 4.1).

Heuristically, the Poisson formula $E(\mathcal F_{e_{\mathbb R}}f)(x)=E(f)(x^{-1})$, $E(f)(x)=|x|^{1/2}\sum_{n>0}f(nx)$, shows that in Fourier (Mellin) variables $E$ is multiplication by $\zeta(\frac12-is)$ and the composite $I\circ\mathcal F$ is multiplication by $u(s)=\zeta(\frac12-is)/\zeta(\frac12+is)$, the ratio (3.4) of archimedean local factors; semi-locally $\sum_{M_S}m^{-1/2+is}=\zeta(\frac12-is)\prod_{p\in S}(1-p^{-1/2+is})$. Kahane's construction of elements of the Sonine space: $D(\Pi)$, $\Pi=\sum\delta_n$, with $D(f)(x)=x^2f''(x)+2xf'(x)$ (symmetric under Fourier), has range in $\{f(0)=\hat f(0)=0\}$.
hypotheses: formal level, technical points ignored (stated by the authors)

statement: Equivalence of (i) $Pu^*(1-P)uP=-\frac12u^{-1}d^-u$, (ii) $u^{-1}d^-u\le0$, (iii) $Pu=PuP$.
role: Gives the precise criterion (u* inner, Beurling) under which a Li-type positivity argument works; used to show it fails.

statement: For $\alpha=\prod_{v\in S}\alpha_v$, the Fourier transform $\mathcal F_\alpha$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb A_S)$ extends uniquely to a unitary operator on $L^2(X_S)$.
role: Hilbert-space set-up for the semi-local framework.

statement: Semi-local sums over $M_S$ (positive integers prime to $S$) reduce, for the trivial character, to $\zeta(\frac12-is)\prod_{p\in S}(1-p^{-1/2+is})$ (referred to in Sect. 4.1).
role: Explains the appearance of local-factor ratios via the Poisson formula.

statement: Let $0<r<1/4$, $f$ non-vanishing continuous on $|z|\le (r+1/4)/2$ and holomorphic in the interior, and $\omega$ real-valued $C^1$ with compact support. Then $\frac1T\int_T^{2T}\omega\big(\max_{|z|\le r}|\zeta(\tfrac34+it+z)-f(z)|\big)dt=\mathbb E\,\omega\big(\max_{|z|\le r}|\zeta(\tfrac34+z,X)-f(z)|\big)+O\big((\log T)^{-\frac{3/4-r}{11}+o(1)}\big)$, implied constant depending on $f,\omega,r$.

kind: corollary (conditional on regularity of limit law)
statement: If $Y_{r,f}=\max_{|z|\le r}|\zeta(\tfrac34+z,X)-f(z)|$ is absolutely continuous, then for fixed $\varepsilon>0$: $\frac1T\mathrm{meas}\{t\in[T,2T]:\max|\zeta(\tfrac34+it+z)-f(z)|<\varepsilon\}=\mathbb P(Y_{r,f}<\varepsilon+O((\log T)^{-(3/4-r)/11+o(1)}))$.
hypotheses: absolute continuity of Y_{r,f} (authors cannot even show absence of jump discontinuities; conjectured)

statement: For fixed $0<r<1/4$ there are $b_1,b_2,b_3>0$ depending only on $r$ such that with $\sigma(r)=3/4-r$: $\mathbb P_T\big(\max_{|z|\le r}|\zeta'(\tfrac34+it+z)|>e^V\big)\ll\exp\big(-b_1V^{\frac1{1-\sigma(r)}}(\log V)^{\frac{\sigma(r)}{1-\sigma(r)}}\big)$ uniformly for $b_2<V\le b_3(\log T)^{1-\sigma}/\log\log T$.
Same tail bound for the random model: $\mathbb P(\max_{|z|\le r}|\zeta'(\tfrac34+z,X)|>e^V)\ll\exp(-b_1V^{1/(1-\sigma(r))}(\log V)^{\sigma(r)/(1-\sigma(r))})$ for all $V>b_2$.

Fix $1/2<\sigma_0<1$; $s_j,r_j$ in $\sigma_0<\mathrm{Re}<1$, $|\mathrm{Im}|\le T^{(\sigma_0-1/2)/4}$. There are $c_3,c_4,c_5>0$ and $E(T)\subset[T,2T]$ with $\mathrm{meas}\,E(T)\ll T^{1-c_3}$ such that for $k,\ell\le c_4\log T/\log\log T$: $\frac1T\int_{[T,2T]\setminus E(T)}\prod_{j\le k}\log\zeta(s_j+it)\prod_{j\le\ell}\overline{\log\zeta(r_j+it)}\,dt=\mathbb E[\prod\log\zeta(s_j,X)\prod\overline{\log\zeta(r_j,X)}]+O(T^{-c_5})$ (the displayed integrand in the text uses $\log\zeta(r_j-it)$, i.e. conjugates).

Fix $1/2<\sigma<1$, $J\le(\log T)^\sigma$, $s_j$ with $\min\mathrm{Re}\,s_j=\sigma$, $\max|\mathrm{Im}\,s_j|<T^{(\sigma-1/2)/4}$. There are $c_1(\sigma),c_2(\sigma)>0$ such that for $\max|u_j|,\max|v_j|\le c_1(\sigma)(\log T)^\sigma/J$: $\Phi_T(u,v)=\Phi_{rand}(u,v)+O(\exp(-c_2(\sigma)\log T/\log\log T))$, with $\Phi$ the joint characteristic functions of $(\mathrm{Re},\mathrm{Im})\log\zeta(s_j+it)$ resp. $\log\zeta(s_j,X)$.

Let $1/2<\sigma=\min\mathrm{Re}\,s_j\le\max\mathrm{Re}\,s_j<1$, $\max|\mathrm{Im}\,s_j|<T^{(\sigma-1/2)/4}$, $J\le(\log T)^{\sigma/2}$. Then the rectangle discrepancy $D_T(s_1,\dots,s_J)=\sup_{R_j}|\mathbb P_T(\log\zeta(s_j+it)\in R_j\forall j)-\mathbb P(\log\zeta(s_j,X)\in R_j\forall j)|\ll J^2/(\log T)^\sigma$.
location: Sec. 2, Thm 2.3 (proved in Sec. 7, via Beurling-Selberg functions)

statement: For $0<r<1/4$, $J\le(\log T)^{(3/4-r)/7}$, $|z_j|\le r$: $|\mathbb P_T(\max_{j\le J}|\zeta(\tfrac34+it+z_j)-f(z_j)|\le u)-\mathbb P(\max_j|\zeta(\tfrac34+z_j,X)-f(z_j)|\le u)|\ll u\,(J\log\log T)^{6/5}/(\log T)^{(3/4-r)/5}$.
Statement concerns $0<r<1/4$, $\delta=(1/4-r)/4$, $y\le\log T$ (Dirichlet-polynomial approximation setup for zeta' near sigma=3/4-r); exact statement not extracted.
role: Input to Prop 2.1: controls max of zeta' via short Euler/Dirichlet polynomial plus zero-density to exclude zeros.

statement: Imported approximation of log zeta(s) by a Dirichlet polynomial over primes up to y for y>=2, |t|>=y+3 (outside a zero-free rectangle).
role: Standard Selberg/Granville-Soundararajan-style approximation used for both Prop 2.1 and moments.

statement: Exceptional set $E(T)\subset[T,2T]$ of measure $\ll T^{1-c}$ outside which zeta has no zeros in relevant rectangles around $s_j+it$ (zero-density input).
role: Allows log zeta to be defined and approximated, and gives Theorem 2.1 away from E(T).

statement: $|F_I(x)|\le1$ for the Beurling-Selberg Fourier-side test functions $F_I$.
role: Bounds in the discrepancy argument converting characteristic function closeness (Thm 2.2) to rectangle discrepancy (Thm 2.3).

statement: $\max_j|\zeta(\tfrac34+it+z_j)-f(z_j)|\le\max_{|z|\le r}|\cdots|\le\max_j\max_{z\in D_j}|\cdots|$ with $D_j$ discs of radius eps covering $|z|=r$, $J\asymp1/\varepsilon$.
role: Reduces the sup over a disc to finitely many (growing with T) shifts; derivative bound (Prop 2.1) shows the two sides agree off a small set.

statement: Let $q$ be odd and fixed, $X(s)=q^{-1/2+s}$, $X_D(s)=|D|^{1/2-s}X(s)$ (so $L(s,\chi_D)=X_D(s)L(1-s,\chi_D)$ for $D\in\mathcal H_{2g+1,q}$). Then for fixed integer $k\ge1$, as $g\to\infty$: $\sum_{D\in\mathcal H_{2g+1,q}}L(\tfrac12,\chi_D)^k=\sum_{D}Q_k(\log_q|D|)(1+o(1))$, where $Q_k$ is a polynomial of degree $k(k+1)/2$ given by the $k$-fold residue $Q_k(x)=\frac{(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}2^k}{k!}\frac{1}{(2\pi i)^k}\oint\!\cdots\!\oint \frac{G(z_1,\dots,z_k)\Delta(z_1^2,\dots,z_k^2)^2}{\prod_j z_j^{2k-1}}q^{\frac x2\sum_j z_j}\,dz_1\cdots dz_k$, with $G=A(\tfrac12;z)\prod_j X(\tfrac12+z_j)^{-1/2}\prod_{i\le j}\zeta_A(1+z_i+z_j)$, $\zeta_A(s)=(1-q^{1-s})^{-1}$, and $A(\tfrac12;z)$ the Euler product (3.6) over monic irreducible $P$ (absolutely convergent for $|\Re z_j|<\tfrac12$).
hypotheses: q odd and fixed; g->infinity (not the Katz-Sarnak q->infinity limit)
conditional_on: unproved CFKRS recipe (stated in Sec. 4 as used 'without rigorous justification in each step')

statement: For $k=1$ the conjecture reduces to $Q_1(x)=ax+b$ and coincides with the first-moment theorem of Andrade-Keating [AK] (imported, unconditional result for $\sum_{D\in\mathcal H_{2g+1,q}}L(1/2,\chi_D)$ with main term of size $|D|\log_q|D|/\zeta_A(2)$ times a constant; the explicit constant was not independently verified by me).

Second moment: $\sum_{D}L(\tfrac12,\chi_D)^2=\sum_D Q_2(\log_q|D|)(1+o(1))$ with $Q_2$ cubic, leading term involving $A(\tfrac12;0,0)=\prod_P\bigl(1-\frac{4|P|^2-3|P|+1}{|P|^4+|P|^3}\bigr)$ (function-field analogue of Jutila's constant (1.14)).

Third moment leading order: $\sum_{D\in\mathcal H_{2g+1,q}}L(\tfrac12,\chi_D)^3\sim\frac{1}{2880\,\zeta_A(2)}A(\tfrac12;0,0,0)\,|D|(\log_q|D|)^6$, with $A(\tfrac12;0,0,0)=\prod_P\bigl(1-\frac{12|P|^5-23|P|^4+23|P|^3-15|P|^2+6|P|-1}{|P|^6(|P|+1)}\bigr)$, matching the shape of Soundararajan's number-field constant (1.15). The coefficient list was obtained by Mathematica (5.26).
location: Sec. 5.3 (eq. 5.27 writes A(1/2;0,0) where A(1/2;0,0,0) is meant: typo)

statement: Assuming Conjecture 5, for each fixed $k\in\mathbb N$, as $g\to\infty$: $\sum_{D\in\mathcal H_{2g+1,q}}L(\tfrac12,\chi_D)^k\sim\frac{|D|}{\zeta_A(2)}(\log_q|D|)^{k(k+1)/2}A(\tfrac12;0,\dots,0)\prod_{j=1}^k\frac{j!}{(2j)!}$. (For k=3, $\prod j!/(2j)!=1/2880$, consistent with 5.27.)
location: Sec. 5.4, eq. (5.29); proof via Lemma 5 (follows Keating-Odgers [KO])

statement: For $\Re\alpha_k,\Re\gamma_m>0$ (with the usual size restrictions): $\sum_{D\in\mathcal H_{2g+1,q}}\prod_{k=1}^K L(\tfrac12+\alpha_k,\chi_D)\big/\prod_{m=1}^Q L(\tfrac12+\gamma_m,\chi_D)=\sum_D\sum_{\epsilon\in\{\pm1\}^K}|D|^{\frac12\sum_k(\epsilon_k\alpha_k-\alpha_k)}\prod_k X(\tfrac12+\tfrac{\alpha_k-\epsilon_k\alpha_k}{2})\,Y(\epsilon\alpha;\gamma)A_D(\epsilon\alpha;\gamma)+o(|D|)$ with $Y$ the $\zeta_A$-ratio (3.9) and $A_D$ the Euler product (3.8). Conjecture 7 is the equivalent K-fold contour-integral form over $|z_i|=1$ with kernel $\Delta(z^2)^2\prod z_k/\prod_{j,k}(z_k-\alpha_j)(z_k+\alpha_j)$.
hypotheses: real parts of alpha_k, gamma_m positive

statement: For $-\tfrac14<\Re\alpha<\tfrac14$, $\tfrac1{\log|D|}\ll\Re\gamma<\tfrac14$, $\Im\alpha,\Im\gamma\ll_\varepsilon|D|^{1-\varepsilon}$: $\sum_D\frac{L(\frac12+\alpha,\chi_D)}{L(\frac12+\gamma,\chi_D)}=\sum_D\Bigl(\frac{\zeta_A(1+2\alpha)}{\zeta_A(1+\alpha+\gamma)}A_D(\alpha;\gamma)+|D|^{-\alpha}X(\tfrac12+\alpha)\frac{\zeta_A(1-2\alpha)}{\zeta_A(1-\alpha+\gamma)}A_D(-\alpha;\gamma)\Bigr)+o(|D|)$.

Theorem 2: under Conj. 8, $\sum_D L'/L(\tfrac12+r,\chi_D)=\sum_D\bigl[\frac{\zeta_A'}{\zeta_A}(1+2r)+A_D'(r;r)-(\log q)|D|^{-r}X(\tfrac12+r)\zeta_A(1-2r)A_D(-r;r)\bigr]$ (error o(|D|)). Theorem 3: for even periodic nice test function $f$ the one-level density $S_1(f)=\sum_D\sum_{\gamma_D}f(\gamma_D)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi/\log q}^{\pi/\log q}f(t)\sum_D\bigl[\log|D|+\frac{X'}{X}\text{-term}+2\frac{\zeta_A'}{\zeta_A}(1+2it)+A_D'(it;it)-(\log q)|D|^{-it}X(\tfrac12+it)\zeta_A(1-2it)A_D(-it;it)\bigr]dt+o(|D|)$ (precise form eq. 7.17), with $A_D(r;r)=1$ and the explicit $A_D'(r;r)=\sum_P\frac{\log|P|}{(|P|^{1+2r}-1)(|P|+1)}$.

Let $F$ be symmetric in $k$ variables, regular near 0, and $f$ have a simple pole of residue 1 at $0$, otherwise analytic nearby. With $K(|D|;w)=\sum_{\epsilon_j=\pm1}e^{\frac12\log|D|\sum\epsilon_jw_j}F(\epsilon w)\prod_{i\le j}f(\epsilon_iw_i+\epsilon_jw_j)$ and $I(|D|,k;0)$ its value at $w=0$: $I(|D|,k;0)\sim(\tfrac12\log|D|)^{k(k+1)/2}F(0,\dots,0)2^{k(k+1)/2}\prod_{j=1}^k\frac{j!}{(2j)!}$.
role: Extracts the leading coefficient of the k-th moment conjecture; imported-style computation following Keating-Odgers [KO] and CFKRS Lemma 2.5.2

statement: Conjecture B implies Artin's conjecture: for K/k Galois and $\rho\neq1$ irreducible, $L(s,\rho,K/k)$ is entire.
hypotheses: Selberg Conjecture B (primitive F: $n_F=1$; distinct primitives orthogonal)

statement: Let K/Q be Galois and $\chi$ an irreducible character of $\mathrm{Gal}(K/\mathbb Q)$. Conjecture B implies $L(s,\chi)$ is primitive.

Assume Conjecture B. Let K/Q be Galois with solvable group G and $\chi$ irreducible of degree n. Then there is an irreducible cuspidal automorphic representation $\pi$ of $GL_n(\mathbb A_{\mathbb Q})$ with $L(s,\chi)=L(s,\pi)$.
conditional_on: Arthur-Clozel base change/automorphic induction for cyclic prime degree

statement: (a) If $F=F_1^{e_1}\cdots F_r^{e_r}$ with $F_i$ primitive then Conjecture B implies $n_F=\sum e_i^2$. (b) Conjecture B implies F primitive iff $n_F=1$.
If K/Q is arbitrary Galois and $\zeta_K$ is automorphic, Conjecture B implies Langlands reciprocity for Gal(K/Q) in the same way.
Conjecture B implies every F in S has unique factorization into primitives.
role: Core of Thm 3.1: compare factorizations of $L(s,\chi_1)/L(s,\chi_2)$.

statement: Assume Conjecture B. If $\pi$ is irreducible cuspidal on $GL_n(\mathbb A_{\mathbb Q})$ satisfying Ramanujan, then $L(s,\pi)$ is primitive.
role: Identifies automorphic L-functions with primitives; uses Rankin-Selberg (Jacquet-Shalika, Shahidi) for prime sum asymptotics (note: this part is unconditional) and Prop 2.5(b).

statement: Base change and automorphic induction exist for cyclic prime-degree extensions (imported).
role: Imported theorem enabling solvable case.

statement: For $t>1$ and $\varepsilon>0$: $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)=O(t^{\theta+\varepsilon})$ with $\theta=9/56=0.16071\ldots$, the implied constant depending on $\varepsilon$ alone.

Let $A,C>1$, $\Delta_1,\Delta_2>0$, and let $\mathcal N(\Delta_1,\Delta_2;A,C)$ be the number of pairs $\{a/c,a_1/c_1\}$ with $a,a_1\sim A$, $c,c_1\sim C$, $(a,c)=(a_1,c_1)=1$, $\|\bar a/c-\bar a_1/c_1\|<\Delta_1$ and $|ac-a_1c_1|<\Delta_2AC$ (where $\bar a$ is the inverse of $a$ mod $c$, $\|\cdot\|$ the distance to the nearest integer). Then $\mathcal N\ll(AC+\Delta_1\Delta_2A^2C^2+\Delta_1^2A^2C+\Delta_2A^2+\Delta_2C^2)(AC)^\varepsilon$, with the implied constant depending on $\varepsilon$ and on the constants implied in $\sim$.

Generalization of Theorem 4.1 to fractions in $\mathscr P(r,s)=\{a/c: a\sim A,\ c\sim C,\ (a,c)=1,\ a=O(\cdot r),\ c=O(\cdot s)\}$ for coprime $r,s$, proved by induction on $rs$. Theorem 4.1 is the case $r=s=1$. The displayed bound was not read in OCR; see the page image.

If $f$ is smooth with $|f^{(j)}(m)|\sim FM^{-j}$ for $m\sim M$, $j\ge1$, and $F^{3/7}<M<F^{1/2}$, then $S_f(M)=\sum_{m\sim M}e(f(m))\ll F^{\theta+\varepsilon}M^{1/2}$ with $\theta=9/56$. Together with the exponent pair $(1/9,13/18)$ for $1<M<F^{3/7}$ this gives $M^{1/2}F^{10/63}$, which is stronger than (5.4) there. The theorem follows from these via the standard approximation, Titchmarsh [9].

Bilinear-form large-sieve-type inequality for sums over points $\xi\in\mathbb R^K$, $\eta\in\mathbb R^K$ with spacing/box parameters, derived from Lemma 2.3 (Beurling-Selberg majorant, via Vaaler). The displayed inequality was lost in OCR.
role: Bounds the bilinear form arising after Holder in Sec. 5 by counting close pairs.

statement: Airy-Hardy integral estimate, stationary-phase style estimates for Poisson summation (2.6-2.8), Poisson summation mod c (2.9), Gauss sum evaluation G(a,l;c) (2.10).
role: Technical tools for completing and evaluating the incomplete Gauss sum.

statement: Asymptotic evaluation of the perturbed incomplete Gauss sum $S(\mu;a,b;c)$ mod c via Poisson summation, with error $\ll c^{-1/2}\sum_h(\ldots)$ and a main term from the Gauss sums $G(a,h;c)$.
role: Replaces Weyl's repeated Cauchy step by evaluation of the Gauss sum; this is the key new idea.

statement: Count 'trivial' pairs (Lemma 4.1), pairs differing by an SL(2,Z) transformation with small matrix (Lemma 4.2), and a Cauchy reduction for induction (Lemma 4.3).
role: Inductive proof of Theorem 4.2.

statement: Bound $\mathscr B(a;\mathfrak D)\ll H^{4+\varepsilon}$, imported from the companion paper [1], Bombieri-Iwaniec, Some mean-value theorems for exponential sums, same volume, pp.473-486.
role: Handles the second system of conditions in the Holder step.

statement: Assume q=p^{a} with a even (i.e. q a square, in the paper's notation q=p^a with a even) and q>(g+1)^4. Then \nu_1(C)\le q+1+(2g+1)\sqrt q. (The displayed bound is missing from the text layer; this is the standard form and is consistent with the proof's conclusion in Section II, but it was not directly checked on the scan.)

The Riemann hypothesis for C/F_q, namely |\omega_i|=\sqrt q for the Frobenius eigenvalues, follows from the upper bound \nu_r(C)\le q^r+O(q^{r/2}) valid after base-field extensions for all r, combined with a lower bound obtained from a Galois-cover argument; the paper states one needs a lower bound for \nu_1 too since the upper bound alone is consistent with \omega_1=q,\omega_2=1.
hypotheses: after replacing F_q by an extension so that q is an even power of p
approximation argument: it suffices to prove \nu_1 \ge q+1-O(\sqrt q) uniformly in the extension (displayed in the paper, not legible in the text layer)

statement: With R_m the space of rational functions on C with poles bounded by m x_0 (x_0 an F_q-rational point), R_m^{(q)} the span of q-th powers, and the Frobenius \varphi: if \ell p^{?}<q (the text reads 'if l\mu<q'), then the natural homomorphism R_\ell \otimes R_m^{(q)}\to R_{\ell+qm} (the multiplication map on products f\cdot h^q) is an isomorphism (injective). The displayed condition is partly garbled in the text layer.
role: Replaces the hyperderivative construction of Stepanov and Schmidt by a pure dimension-count and pole-order argument at x_0, so that the auxiliary function exists with controlled poles.

statement: If 4pl'<q (garbled), then the product space map has dimension (\dim R_\ell)(\dim R_m)=\ldots, equal to the dimension of the image, consequence of (vi) which is not legible.
role: Gives the dimension count (via Riemann-Roch: \dim R_m=m+1-g for m>2g-2) showing the kernel of the induced map \delta is large enough to produce a nonzero f vanishing to high order at all rational points.

statement: (i) \dim R_m\le m+1; (ii) \dim R_m\ge m+1-g with equality for m>2g-2; (iii) \dim R_{m+1}\le\dim R_m+1 (increments at most 1); (iv) R_m^{p}\circ\varphi-type containment R_m\circ\varphi\subset R_{mq}; (v) every element of R_m\circ\varphi is a q-th power.
role: Basic Riemann-Roch input for dimension counts; (iv)-(v) bring in Frobenius.

statement: Choose a separable k(C)/k(t); take its Galois closure C'\to\mathbb{P}^1 with group G and subgroup H; for each \sigma\in G the number of points of C' with Frobenius substitution \sigma satisfies an upper bound from the Theorem-1-type argument applied to C' with twisted Frobenius, and the sum over all \sigma of these counts is q+O(1) (branch points), which forces each count to be q+O(\sqrt q) and gives the lower bound.
role: Supplies the lower bound for \nu_1 from upper bounds for all twisted point counts, a Chebotarev-type trick.

statement: For at least 87.5% of odd square-free $d\ge0$, $L(\tfrac12,\chi_{8d})\ne0$: for all large $x$ and any fixed $\varepsilon>0$, $\sum_{\substack{d\le x\\L(1/2,\chi_{8d})\ne0}}\mu(2d)^2\ge(\tfrac78-\varepsilon)\sum_{d\le x}\mu(2d)^2$.
There is a degree-3 polynomial Q with $\sum_{0\le d\le X}L(\tfrac12,\chi_{8d})^2=XQ(\log X)+O(X^{5/6+\varepsilon})$, sum over fundamental discriminants $8d$.
There is a degree-6 polynomial R with $\sum_{0\le d\le X}L(\tfrac12,\chi_{8d})^3=XR(\log X)+O(X^{11/12+\varepsilon})$, sum over fundamental discriminants $8d$ (sketch only, Sec. 7).

If $M(d)=\sum_{l\le M}\lambda(l)\sqrt l\,(\tfrac{8d}{l})$ with $\lambda(l)\ll l^{-1+\varepsilon}$, then for $j=1,2$: $S_R(|M(d)^jA_j(d)|;\Phi)\ll\big(\tfrac{X^\varepsilon}{Y}+\tfrac{M^{2}}{X^{1/2-\varepsilon}}\big)^{j}$-type bound (exact form per source p.451: $\ll (X^\varepsilon/Y + M^2/X^{1/2-\varepsilon})$ to power structure garbled in extraction).

For odd $l=l_1l_2^2$, $l_1$ square-free: $2S_M(\tfrac{8d}{l}A_1(d);\Phi)=\frac{\hat\Phi(0)C}{\zeta(2)}\frac{\sqrt{l}}{... l_1 g(l)}\Big(\log\frac{X}{l_1}+C_2+\sum_{p|l}\frac{C_2(p)}{p}\log p\Big)+O\big(\ldots\big)$ (main term as in p.452; error uses $Y$, $X^{1/2-\varepsilon}$), with $C=\frac13\prod_{p\ge3}(1-\frac1{p(p+1)})$, $g(l)=\prod_{p|l}\frac{p+1}{p}(1-\frac1{p(p+1)})$. Exact formula only partially captured by text extraction.

Second mollified-moment asymptotic for $2S_M(\tfrac{8d}{l}A_2(d);\Phi)$ with main term $\frac{D\hat\Phi(0)}{36\zeta(2)}\frac{d(l_1)}{\sqrt{l_1}\sigma(l_1)h(l)}\big(\log^3\frac{X}{l_1}-\ldots\big)$ plus lower-order terms $O(l)$ with polynomials $Q_{j,k}$ of degree <=2, plus remainder $R(l)$, $|R(l)|\ll \ldots l^{1/2+\varepsilon}Y^{1+\varepsilon}/X^{1/2-\varepsilon}$ pointwise and $\sum_{L\le l<2L}|R(l)|\ll\ldots L^{1+\varepsilon}Y^{1+\varepsilon}/X^{1/2-\varepsilon}$ on average.

With mollifier length $\sqrt X^{\theta}$ (i.e. $M=X^{\theta/2}$), the optimal mollifier yields proportion $\ge1-(\theta+1)^{-3}+o(1)$; Props 1.2-1.3 allow $\theta=1-\varepsilon$ giving 7/8. Arbitrary length ($\theta\to\infty$) would give almost all.
hypotheses: mollifier length limited by error terms of Props 1.1-1.3

statement: For odd positive square-free d and $j\ge1$: $L(\tfrac12,\chi_{8d})^j=2A_j(d)$ with $A_j(d)=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(8d/n)d_j(n)}{\sqrt n^{\,j}}\omega_j\big(\frac{n\pi}{8d}\big)$-type smoothed sum (def. (1.6)).
role: Approximate functional equation for L and L^2 (the real character gives root number 1).

statement: Heath-Brown large sieve for real characters: $\sum_{\chi\in S(Q)}|\sum_{n\le N}a_n\chi(n)|^2\ll_\varepsilon(QN)^\varepsilon(Q+N)\sum_{n_1n_2=\square}|a_{n_1}a_{n_2}|$, S(Q)= real primitive characters of conductor <=Q.
role: Bounds non-principal character sums in the off-diagonal terms.

statement: For $\sigma\ge1/2$: $\sum_{\chi\in S(Q)}|L(\sigma+it,\chi)|^4\ll Q^{1+\varepsilon}(1+|t|)^{1+\varepsilon}$ and the square-moment analog with $(1+|t|)^{1/2+\varepsilon}$.
role: Controls the tail terms/remainders.

statement: For F nonnegative smooth supported in (1,2) and odd n: $S_M(\tfrac dn;F)=\frac{1}{2n}\frac Xn... \sum_{\alpha\le Y,(\alpha,2n)=1}\frac{\mu(\alpha)}{\alpha^2}\sum_k(-1)^kG_k(n)\tilde F\big(\frac{kX}{2\alpha^2n}\big)$ (Poisson summation with Gauss sums $G_k(n)$).
role: Converts the character sum over d to a dual sum in which the k=square terms give the off-diagonal contribution.

statement: Polya-Vinogradov-based bound for $S_M(\tfrac{8d}{ln};\Phi_n)$ when $ln\ne\square$.
role: Shows only $ln=\square$ terms contribute to the first moment (Prop 1.2).

statement: Analysis of Dirichlet series of Gauss-sum weights and estimation of the k=square off-diagonal terms (Sec. 5.3).
role: Evaluate the nondiagonal contribution: the most delicate part of the argument.

statement: Let L=\log(T/2\pi) and U=T/L^{10}. For all sufficiently large T, N_0(T+U)-N_0(T)>\tfrac13\,[N(T+U)-N(T)], where N_0(T) counts zeros of \zeta(1/2+it) with 0<t\le T and N(T)=\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi}-\frac{T}{2\pi}+O(\log T) counts all zeros in 0<\sigma<1,0<t<T. The proof actually yields the lower bound 0.34\,UL/(2\pi).
hypotheses: N_0 counting convention (with or without multiplicity) is not spelled out in the intro; the proof tracks multiplicity (zeros of G of order k give zeros of zeta of order k+1)
location: Section 1, p. 384; proof in Section 15, pp. 433-435

label_in_source: Corollary (p. 384, due to H. L. Montgomery)
statement: If m denotes the multiplicity of a zero of \zeta on \sigma=1/2, then \sum (m-1) over zeros with 1/2+iT\le \rho\le 1/2+i(T+U) is bounded by N_G(D)<0.329\,UL/(2\pi) (from (15.4)); hence \sum_{m\ge2} m is a small multiple (<~ 2 times that) of UL. The constants in the printed statement are garbled in OCR ('C(m-1)<G log g').
location: p. 384; proof at end of Section 15

statement: With G(s)=\zeta(s)+\frac{\zeta'(s)}{f'(s)+f'(1-s)} and D the rectangle with vertices 1/2+iT, 3+iT, 3+i(T+U), 1/2+i(T+U): \arg G(1/2+it)\big|_T^{T+U}=-2\pi N_G(D)+O(L), where N_G(D) is the number of zeros of G in D.

With y=T^{1/2}/L^{20}, mollifier \psi (Dirichlet polynomial of length y built from the Mobius function with smoothing weights, defined in (2.3)-(2.4)), a=1/2-R/L and R fixed: \int_T^{T+U}|\psi G(a+it)|^2dt=U\,F(R)+O(U\log^5L/L), with F(R)=e^{2R}(\cdots) (explicit expression (15.1)). For R=1.3: F(1.3)<2.3502, giving (1/2-a)\,2\pi N_G(D)<0.4275\,U, i.e. 2\pi N_G(D)<0.329\,UL.

Zeros of \zeta(1/2+it) occur where \arg\{h(s)\,[\,(f'(s)+f'(1-s))\zeta(s)+\zeta'(s)\,]\}\equiv\pi/2\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \pi) on \sigma=1/2 (h(s)=\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)); so it suffices to control the argument change of G(s) on the half line.
role: Converts zero counting for zeta on the critical line into winding of G; argument change on the line is dominated by zeros of G in D.

statement: For F analytic in D_a, \int_T^{T+U}\log|F(a+it)|dt-\int_T^{T+U}\log|F(3+it)|dt+\int_a^3\arg F(\sigma+i(T+U))d\sigma-\int_a^3\arg F(\sigma+iT)d\sigma=2\pi\sum\mathrm{dist}; applied to \psi G with concavity \int\log|\psi G|\le \frac U2\log(\frac1U\int|\psi G|^2).
role: Bounds N_G(D) by a mollified mean square of G on the line sigma=a slightly left of 1/2; the mollifier flattens |zeta| to make Jensen sharp.

statement: Via the Riemann-Siegel formula, G(\sigma+it)=H(\sigma+it)+H_1(t) with H_1(t)=O(t^{-1/4}) and H=\ldots built from g_1,g_2,g_3 (sums over n<(t/2\pi)^{1/2}) and \chi_1(t); then \int|\psi G|^2=\int|\psi H|^2+O(U^{1/2})+\ldots
role: Reduces the mean square to Dirichlet polynomials of length ~T^{1/2}.

statement: For 1\le A_1,A_2\le T^{1/2}, (A_1,A_2)=1, off-diagonal sum over j_1,j_2 with A_1j_1\ne A_2j_2 satisfies a bound <100\,T^{1-2a}\log T (precise form (3.2) garbled).
role: Off-diagonal (Montgomery-Vaughan-type) control in the mean square.

statement: Lemma 3.4: \int_A^B\exp[it\log(t/ye)](t/2\pi)^{1/2-a}dt=(2\pi)^a y^{1-a}e^{-iy+\pi i/4}+E(y) for A<y<B<A+A/\log A (analogue of Selberg 1942 Lemma 2); Lemma 3.5 handles the same for m=1,2.
role: Stationary-phase evaluation of the main oscillatory integrals arising from the Riemann-Siegel main sum.

statement: Lemma 3.6: \sum_{k|k_1,k_2}\ldots with k=(k_1,k_2): \sum k/(k_1k_2)\ldots=O(\log^3 y). Lemma 3.7: lattice-point count \sum_{(n,m)\in K}f(n,m)=\iint_K f\,du\,dv+\mathcal J with explicit error for a region in the first quadrant (Euler-Maclaurin in two variables).
role: Combinatorial and lattice tools for evaluating the double sums over mollifier coefficients.

statement: Lemma 3.8 (Mobius inversion of g(m)=\sum_{r|m}\mu(r)f(rm)-type); Lemma 3.9: for large squarefree j, \sum_{p|j}\frac{\log p}{p}=O(\log\log j); Lemma 3.11: J(x)=\sum_{r\le x}\mu^2(r)\prod_{p|r}f(p)/r \cdots=\prod_p(1+\tfrac{1}{p}\ldots)(1-\tfrac1p)\log x+O(1) for f(p)=1+O(p^{-c}); Lemmas 3.12-3.13 variants.
role: Evaluation of the arithmetic sums (singular series) that give the explicit value F(R).

statement: If zeta has a zero of multiplicity m on sigma=1/2 then G has one of multiplicity m-1; each zero of G on the line gives a zero of zeta of one higher multiplicity; counting the argument variation of G on intervals between indentations at the N_1' zeros on the line gives at least UL/(2\pi)\cdot(1-2\cdot0.329)>0.34\,UL/(2\pi) zeros of zeta on the line.
role: Final bookkeeping from argument variation of G to the count N_0 (including zeros of G on the line and multiplicity).

label_in_source: Hauptsatz (stated in the introduction p. 255 and proved in Sec. 4, pp. 271-274)
statement: For every fixed $\sigma_0$ with $\tfrac12<\sigma_0\le1$ (the table of contents gives the range as 1/2<sigma_0<=1; the sentence stating the theorem in the OCR reads 1/2<sigma_0<1 with equality allowed per the introduction, which treats $\sigma=1$ explicitly), the set $\{\zeta(\sigma_0+it):t\in\mathbb R\}$ is dense in $\mathbb C$: for every $a\in\mathbb C$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is $t_0$ with $|\zeta(\sigma_0+it_0)-a|<\varepsilon$.
hypotheses: t ranges over R (both signs of t used; the proof picks t_0 in (0,T) after discarding the negative-t part)

label_in_source: Introduction pp. 249-251 (recalled earlier result of Bohr)
statement: For fixed $\sigma_0>1$ the set $U(\sigma_0)=\{\prod_n(1-p_n^{-\sigma_0}e^{2\pi i\eta_n})^{-1}\}$ is dense in $V(\sigma_0)=\{\zeta(\sigma_0+it)\}$ closure; and there is $\sigma_0(R)>1$ such that for $1<\sigma_0<\sigma_0(R)$ the circle-multiplication set $F(\sigma_0)$ contains the disc $|z|\le R$, hence the values of $\zeta$ on the line are dense in any bounded region of the plane for $\sigma_0$ close to 1.

Let $\tfrac12<\sigma_0<1$, $\varepsilon,\delta>0$ and $R_N(s)=\zeta(s)\prod_{n\le N}(1-p_n^{-s})$. Then there is $N_0(\sigma_0,\varepsilon,\delta)$ such that for every $N\ge N_0$ the total length $\mu_N(T)$ of the set of $t\in[-T,T]$ with $|R_N(\sigma_0+it)-1|\ge\varepsilon$ is $<\delta T$ for $T\ge T_0(N)$. (The tail product need not converge pointwise but converges 'almost everywhere in measure'.)
role: Controls the remainder: shows the truncated Euler product approximates zeta for most t; proof via Schnee's mean-value theorem for Dirichlet series (imported)

statement: (Kronecker equidistribution in Jordan measure) If $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_N$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$ and $\Omega$ is a Jordan-measurable region in the unit cube $Q$ of volume $W$, then the set $M(T)$ of $t\in[0,T]$ with $(t\lambda_1,\dots,t\lambda_N)\bmod 1\in\Omega$ has $\mu(M(T))/T\to W$. The authors note it fails for Lebesgue measure on non-Jordan measurable sets.
role: Quantifies how often the finite Euler product reaches a region; Weyl's proof (July 1913) is acknowledged

statement: Let $r_n\in(0,1)$ with $\sum r_n$ divergent and $\sum r_n^2$ convergent, and $R_0$ a fixed axis-parallel rectangle with centre $z_0$ in the $z$-plane. Then there is $k=k(R_0,z_0)>0$ and $N_0$ such that for $N\ge N_0$ the probability $W_N(R_0)$ (volume in $\eta\in[0,1]^N$) that the point $S_N(\eta)=\sum_{n\le N}\log(1-r_ne^{2\pi i\eta_n})^{-1}$ lies in $R_0$ is $>k$, with $k$ independent of $N$.
role: Key probabilistic lemma: the sum of logs of the Euler factors (sums of convex closed curves) spreads over the whole plane without the hitting probability for a fixed rectangle tending to 0

kind: theorem (conditional on existence of a CM elliptic curve over Q with analytic order of vanishing g)
statement: Let $E/\mathbb{Q}$ be an elliptic curve with conductor $N$ with complex multiplication, and suppose $L_E(s)$ has a zero of order $g$ at $s=1$. Then for every real primitive Dirichlet character $\chi \pmod d$ with $(d,N)=1$ and $d>\exp\exp(c_1 N g^3)$, $$L(1,\chi) > \frac{c_2}{g^{40g}N^{13}}\cdot\frac{(\log d)^{g-\mu-1}\exp\!\big(-21 g^{3/2}(\log\log d)^{1/2}\big)}{\sqrt d},$$ where $\mu\in\{1,2\}$ is chosen so that $\chi(-N)=(-1)^{g-\mu}$, and $c_1,c_2>0$ are effectively computable and independent of $g,N,d$. (Exact exponent of g in the denominator is read from a low-resolution page image; verify.)
conditional_on: existence of a CM curve with analytic rank g (known only for small g at the time)

statement: Under the hypotheses of Theorem 1, $$L(1,\chi)\gg \frac{g^{-40g}N^{-13}(\log d)^{g-\mu-1}}{\sqrt d\,(\log\log d)^{g-\mu+6}}\prod_{\substack{\chi(p)\ne -1\\ p<(\log d)^{8g}}}(1+p^{-1/2})^{-4}$$ with effective implied constant independent of g,N,d (displayed exponents read from a page image).
For E/Q with CM by an imaginary quadratic field K, $L_E(s)=L(s,\psi)$ for a primitive Grossencharakter $\psi$ of K.

Theorem 1 also holds for non-CM curves if $L_E$ comes from a cusp form of $\Gamma_0(N)$ (Weil's conjecture); more generally for products of Euler factors of elliptic-curve type with zero of order g at s=1 and zero of order related to Tate's conjectures at s=2.

If for Wiman's curve (CM, rank at least 4) one could prove $L_E$ has a zero of order $4$ at $s=1$, then $h(-d)\to\infty$ effectively and the class number problem $h(-d)=\text{const}$ would be effectively solvable.

For $n\le x$ coefficients of the Dirichlet series of the twisted/Liouville-modified function agree with those of $G(s,\chi)q^{-2s}$, where $G$ measures the deviation of $\chi(p)$ from $\lambda(p)=-1$ (statement garbled in OCR).
role: links smallness of L(1,chi) to chi(p)=-1 for most small p

statement: Asymptotic expansions of the Dedekind zeta function $\zeta_K(s)L(s,\chi)$ of imaginary (Thm 3, d>4, chi(-1)=-1) and real (Thm 4, chi(-1)=+1) quadratic fields as sums over reduced forms of discriminant -d / d via Epstein zeta functions (Iseki; Hecke).
role: explicit evaluation of sums of the coefficients $\nu_n$ of $\zeta(s)L(s,\chi)$

statement: For d>4, $\sum_{n<\sqrt d/ 4}\nu_n n^{-1/2}$ is bounded in terms of $L(1,\chi)$ via the class number formula.
role: upper bound feeding Lemma 9

Partial-sum estimates of $
u_n$ with errors expressed via $L(1,\chi)$; Lemma 7: for $x>d>	frac14\sqrt d$ and $10<y<	frac14\sqrt d$, $\sum n^{-1/2}\sum_{m|n,m\le y}
u_m
u_{n/m}\le 1500(L(1,\chi)^2xy^{-1/2}+L(1,\chi)x^{1/2})(\log y)^3$.
role: controls second-moment of nu_n
reduces Theorem 1 to Theorem 5: small L(1,chi) forces chi(p)=-1 for almost all small p, a dichotomy

statement: Lavrik-type approximate functional-equation expansion differentiated K times at s=1/2 splits into T1, T2; Lemma 10: if K<=g, d>exp(500g^3) then |T2|<1; Lemma 11 gives either the target lower bound or a bound on T1.
role: main analytic step; zero of order g at s=1/2 of phi(s) kills the first g derivatives

statement: Statement about primitive Grossencharakter psi of conductor f (used for Sec.5); not read in detail.
role: conductor bookkeeping

statement: For $T>28.558$: $\left|N(T)-\left(\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi}-\frac{T}{2\pi}\right)\right|<0.43200\,\log T+1.91662\,\log\log T+13.07873$, where N(T) counts zeros of xi with Re t in (0,T) with multiplicity (OCR of the constants as read; the main term as in the 1905 claim N=(T/2pi)log(T/2pi)-T/2pi+O(log T)). The previous Mangoldt (1895, J. reine angew. Math. 114, p. 266) bound was $0.34(\log T)^2+1.35\log T+2.58$.
hypotheses: T not the ordinate of a zero (line through T avoids zeros)
location: Math. Ann. 60, p. 1 (introduction), proved on pp. 2-19

statement: Writing the change of arg of xi along the segments from -ia to T-ia to T, 2*pi*N equals twice the increment of the coefficient of i in log xi(t); the first segment's increment Theta_1(a,T) is computed from the Gamma-factor via Stieltjes' formula, giving Theta_1(a,T)=(T/2)log(T/2pi)-T/2+... with explicit remainders.
role: Gamma-factor/Stirling part of the argument principle (explicit S-free part of N(T)).

statement: For the Dirichlet-series/zero part: counts of zeros in windows of length 2k are bounded using the positivity of the increment of the argument of each linear factor (1 - t/t_rho): the number of zeros in an interval of length 2k near height T is bounded by an expression M/(arctg(2k)...) in terms of the increment of the argument over the segment T..T+2k.
role: Bounds the S(T)=arg zeta term (the log T order), by a window-counting device with parameter k.

statement: Optimisation in the free parameter k (called k): the minimiser satisfies $k^2\arctan(2k)$-type equation (22) with root k approx 0.675, giving the constant 0.432 in front of log T (zeta(3)=1.20206 used).
role: Fixes the constants 0.43200, 1.91662, 13.07873.

statement: If F(x)=\sum a_m x^m is entire and |a_m| \le (m!)^{-1/\lambda} (up to epsilon-adjusted form), then F has genus < \lambda in general; the doubtful case is \lambda = E+1 an integer, where genus can be E or E+1. Hadamard states: coefficient of x^m smaller than 1/(m!)^{1/\lambda}-type bound implies genus at most E, E+1 being the least integer exceeding \lambda.
hypotheses: coefficient decay of order (m!)^{-1/\lambda} with \lambda not an integer
location: Introduction p.172; conclusion of Part II no. 33 (as stated: 'la reciproque du theoreme de M. Poincare est donc bien etablie pour lambda non entier'); statement paraphrased from garbled OCR

statement: If |a_m| \le 1/e^{\varphi(m)} with \varphi increasing with m and \varphi(m)/m increasing (after regularising by a convex minorant), then for every \epsilon>0 the maximum modulus satisfies F(x) < A\,x^{\epsilon}e^{\psi(x)}-type bound where \psi is the inverse function of \varphi; i.e. coefficient decay controls growth. Exact displayed form of the bound could not be read in the OCR.

Conversely, from a growth law for F one recovers a coefficient-decay law via Poincare's auxiliary function \Phi(x)=\int_0^\infty e^{-t}F(tx)\,dt generalised to \Phi(x)=\int e^{-\Psi(t)}F(tx)\,dt for general positive increasing \Psi.

Using the limsup determinants of Hadamard's 1892 'Essai sur l'etude des fonctions donnees par leur developpement de Taylor', the successive zeros of an entire function are expressed through its Taylor coefficients; under a regular decay a_m ~ 1/(m!)^{1/\lambda}-type hypothesis this gives the law of distribution of zeros.
hypotheses: regular decay of coefficients, convex regularisation

statement: Picard's theorem (an entire function omits at most one value) is re-derived for all entire functions satisfying the coefficient condition (8), hence for all functions of finite genus.

\sin(\pi x)/(\pi x)=\prod(1-x^2/n^2) with no exponential factor follows from genus zero of the function of x^2 deduced from the Taylor development (a proof that avoids the special argument needed after Weierstrass).

Let \xi(x)=\tfrac12\int ... (Riemann's entire function, defined via \Psi(t)=\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-n^2\pi t}, \xi(x)=\int_1^\infty \Psi(t)\,t^{-3/4}\cos(\tfrac x2\log t)\,dt-type formula (45)-(46)). Considered as a function of x^2, \xi has genus zero; hence \xi(x)=\xi(0)\prod_\alpha(1-x^2/\alpha^2) with no exponential factor. Derived from the coefficient bound of the Taylor expansion in x^2 (condition (8) with exponent \alpha=2-\epsilon, hence \lambda=\tfrac12+\epsilon) combined with the converse-Poincare result.
location: Part III, nos. 34-38 (pp. 210-215); concluding proposition 'La fonction xi(x) (consideree comme fonction de x^2) est de genre zero'

statement: For a coefficient bound |a_m|<=e^{-\varphi(m)}, one may replace \varphi by a function with \varphi(m)/m increasing; for such \varphi, b_{m_0}=m_0(m_0+1)[\varphi(m_0+1)-\varphi(m_0)]-\ldots is increasing and unbounded, and \varphi(m)\ge m^{\lambda'} type growth for any \lambda'>1 slightly above 1 in the relevant normalisation.
role: Regularisation step so that the maximum-term argument of no. 6 applies

statement: For F=e^{G(x)} with G entire, |F| is controlled by Re G; coefficient formula a_m=\frac1{\pi R^m}\int_0^{2\pi}P(Re^{i\theta})\cos m\theta\,d\theta for the real part P of an entire function; if P grows at most polynomially then G is a polynomial of bounded degree.
role: Shows the exponential factor in the Weierstrass product has degree <= E, i.e. G polynomial of degree at most the genus; key to ruling out exp factor

statement: For F with coefficients of order (m!)^{-1/\lambda}, \lambda not an integer, applying the e^{G} analysis to the associated auxiliary function shows G is a polynomial of degree at most E, so F is of genus E, where E+1 is the least integer exceeding \lambda.
role: Delivers the converse of Poincare's theorem (genus vs coefficient decay) in the non-integer case

statement: In the series for \xi in x^2 one may replace \Psi(t) by its first term e^{-\pi t}, drop the factor t^{-3/4}, and observes \log t < \epsilon t^{\,\cdot} for large t, producing Taylor coefficients a_m of size below (m!)^{-(2-\epsilon)}-type in the variable x^2... (exponent reconstructed; OCR garbled).
role: Computes the coefficient decay of xi needed for the genus argument

statement: Let $0<r<\tfrac14$. Let $f(s)$ be analytic in the disc $|s|<r$, continuous on $|s|\le r$, with no zeros in $|s|<r$. Then for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists a real $T$ such that $\max_{|s|\le r}\left|f(s)-\zeta\!\left(s+\tfrac34+iT\right)\right|<\varepsilon$. (The printed text writes the quantifier as 'there exists $T=T(r)$' with a garbled equation; the statement is existence of a shift $T$, with no density statement.)
hypotheses: $f$ analytic in the open disc, continuous up to the boundary

statement: The assertion of the theorem holds for all Dirichlet L-functions (stated without proof).

Under the conditions of the theorem, for every $y>0$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite set $M$ of primes containing all primes $<y$ and real numbers $\theta_k$ (indexed by $p_k$, the $k$th prime) such that the finite Euler product $\prod_{p_k\in M}\left(1-e^{-2\pi i\theta_k}p_k^{-s-3/4}\right)^{-1}$ approximates $f(s)$ on $|s|\le r$ to within $\varepsilon$ (the exact displayed formula is garbled in the extraction; this is the standard form of the lemma and my reading).
role: Approximation of $f$ by finite Euler products with arbitrary phases on primes; then Kronecker/Bohr-type argument transfers to $\zeta(s+3/4+iT)$.

hypotheses: K genus-1 function field over algebraically closed k of characteristic p

statement: N is a positive semidefinite quadratic form on the ring M of meromorphisms: N(\mu\bar\mu - m)=0 for m=N(\mu), and the quadratic polynomial Q(z)=z^2-lz+m (l=\mu+\bar\mu) has discriminant l^2-4m\le0. The quotient ring \Sigma of M is Q, an imaginary quadratic field P(\delta), or an imaginary quadratic division algebra over Q; M is an order in \Sigma.

If k is absolutely algebraic (algebraic closure of \mathbb{F}_p) and \bar\pi\ne\pi (\pi the Frobenius meromorphism (x\pi,y\pi)=(x^q,y^q)), then M is an order in an imaginary quadratic number field in which p splits into two (distinct or equal) prime ideals. The automorphism group is generally cyclic of order 2, order 4 or 6 only for the maximal orders of discriminant -4 or -3. Frobenius satisfies Q(\pi)=\pi^2-l\pi+q=0 with l^2\le4q, N(\pi)=q, J(\pi)=q. Limit cases: (a) \bar\pi=\pi, l=\pm2\sqrt q, \pi^2=q; (b) \bar\pi=-\pi, l=0, \pi^2=-q; they occur iff A=0 (supersingular case); for A\ne0, 0<l^2<4q.
hypotheses: k absolutely algebraic of characteristic p

statement: With K_0=k_0(x,y) of genus 1, L(s)=1-(q+1-N_1)q^{-s}+q^{1-2s}, P(z)=q^{2s}L(s)=z^2-(q+1-N_1)z+q (z=q^s), h=P(1)=N_1 the class number. RH, i.e. (q+1-N_1)^2\le4q, follows from the identity P=Q, which reduces to the single equality N(\pi-1)=h=N_1, proved by counting solutions of (\pi-1)\mathfrak p=\mathfrak o in the divisor class group D_0 of degree-0 classes.
hypotheses: K_0 genus 1 over finite k_0, constant field extension to \bar k_0 irreducible

statement: Replacing z=q^s in P(z) by the Frobenius operator \pi gives a null operator on D_0: P(\pi)\mathfrak p=\pi^2\mathfrak p-(q+1-N_1)\pi\mathfrak p+q\mathfrak p=\mathfrak o. The zeros of L(s) lie on \mathrm{Re}\,s=1/2 in the strip 0\le\mathrm{Im}\,s<2\pi/\log q.
