role: Controls the degree formulas N=N_0 J needed in (1) and in the final identification N(\pi-1)=N_0(\pi-1).

statement: \pi^2=q\zeta with \zeta a normalized automorphism, necessarily a 2nd, 4th or 6th root of unity in P(\pi); if \zeta\ne\pm1 then \pi would have degree >2 over P, contradiction; hence \pi^2=\pm q.
role: Shows limit cases a),b) occur iff A=0.

statement: Since c_{\pi-1}=c_\pi-1=-1\ne0, J(\pi-1)=1 and N(\pi-1)=N_0(\pi-1)= number of \mathfrak p in D_0 with (\pi-1)\mathfrak p=\mathfrak o; by Riemann-Roch each degree-0 class is represented uniquely by \mathfrak p/\mathfrak o with \mathfrak p of degree 1, so h=N_1 equals the same count (fixed points of Frobenius).
role: Key step: relates the degree of Frobenius-minus-one to the point count, giving P(1)=Q(1).

statement: Let $k$ be a global field of characteristic $p>0$. Let $\Sigma_1$ be the set of isomorphism classes of compatible systems of absolutely irreducible 2-dimensional $\lambda$-adic representations of the Weil group $W$ of $k$ ($\lambda\nmid\infty p$, over number fields $E\subset\bar{\mathbb Q}$, $\Sigma_1=\varinjlim\Sigma_1(E)$) and $\Sigma_2$ the set of isomorphism classes of irreducible representations of $GL(2,\mathbb A)$ occurring in the space of cusp forms. Then $\Gamma=\{(\varrho,\pi)\in\Sigma_1\times\Sigma_2:\pi$ compatible with $\varrho\}$ is the graph of a bijection $\Sigma_1\to\Sigma_2$. Compatibility: for almost all places $v$, $L(s-\tfrac12,\pi_v)=[\det(1-F_vq_v^{-s},\varrho_\lambda)]^{-1}$ (Jacquet-Langlands L).
hypotheses: k global function field, char p>0

statement: For an irreducible unitary representation $\pi$ of $GL(2,\mathbb A)$ occurring in the space of cusp forms, for every place $v$ of $k$ the local component $\pi_v$ does not belong to the complementary series.

label_in_source: Theorem C (Riemann hypothesis for $L(s,\pi)$, partly conditional)
statement: Let $\pi$ be as in Theorem B. Suppose either that one of the local components of $\pi$ belongs to the discrete series, or that every field finitely generated and of transcendence degree 3 over $\mathbb F_p$ has a smooth projective model (resolution of singularities in dimension 3). Then all zeros of $L(s,\pi)$ lie on the line $\mathrm{Re}\,s=\tfrac12$.
hypotheses: discrete series local component, or resolution of singularities in dim 3 for char p
conditional_on: resolution of singularities for 3-folds over F_p (second alternative)

statement: For each $\pi\in\Sigma_2$ there exist a number field $E$ containing the field of definition of $\pi$ and 2-dimensional $\lambda$-adic representations $\varrho_\lambda$ of $W$ (for all places $\lambda$ of $E$ not dividing $\infty p$) such that for almost all $v$ and all $\lambda$: $L(s-\tfrac12,\pi_v)=\det(1-F_vq_v^{-s},\varrho_\lambda)^{-1}$. Theorem A follows from A' (0.3).

With $V_i^{cusp}$ the cuspidal part of $\varinjlim_D\,[\prod_n \varinjlim H^i_c(\mathcal N^{2,n}_D\otimes K,\mathbb Q_l)]$, one has $V_1^{cusp}\otimes\bar{\mathbb Q}_l=\bigoplus_{\pi\in\Sigma_2^J}\varrho_\pi\otimes\pi^\vee\otimes\pi$-type decomposition as a representation of $W\times W\times GL(2,\mathbb A)$, where $\Sigma_2^J=\{\pi:\pi|_J$ trivial$\}$ and $\varrho_\pi$ is a 2-dimensional representation of $W$ over $\bar{\mathbb Q}_l$ compatible with $\pi$ (precise form is garbled in OCR).
For every finite subscheme $D\subset X$ and $d\ge1$ the coarse moduli scheme of left (right) F-sheaves of rank d with level D structure exists.
The category of constructible locally constant PF-sheaves of sets on $(X-D)^2$ is equivalent to the category of finite $\pi_1(X-D)\times\pi_1(X-D)$-sets.

There exist open subschemes $U_i\subset M^d_D$ with $U_i\subset U_{i+1}$, $\bigcup U_i=M$, each a quotient of a smooth quasiprojective scheme over $(X-D)^2$ of relative dimension $2d-2$ by a finite group.
role: exhausts the non-quasicompact moduli space of F-sheaves

statement: For $d=1$, $V_i\otimes\bar{\mathbb Q}_l=\bigoplus_{\chi\in\mathrm{Hom}(\mathrm{Pic}_DX/J,\bar{\mathbb Q}_l^*)}\varrho_\chi\boxtimes\varrho_\chi^{-1}\otimes\chi$ type decomposition, with $\varrho_\chi\in\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_1(X-D),\bar{\mathbb Q}_l^*)$ compatible with $\chi$ (class field theory realized geometrically).
role: model case of the whole method

statement: $\mathcal N^{m,n}_D$ is a quasiprojective surface; if $2m-n\ge2$ the complement of $\mathcal N^{m,n}\otimes K$ in the neighbouring piece is a countable disjoint sum of affine lines.
role: describes non-quasicompactness and boundary strata

statement: For $2m-n\ge2$, $\mathcal N^{m,n}_D$ has a canonical compactification $\overline{\mathcal N}^{m,n}_D$ proper normal algebraic space over K; the fibres of a resolution of singularities have $H^0=\bar{\mathbb Q}_l$, $H^1=0$ (trees of rational curves); boundary $\Gamma^{m,n}_D$ described via degenerate F-sheaves (Sec.3.4); for D=0 it is isomorphic as an object of the R-category to $Y^{...}\otimes K$.
role: controls boundary contribution in the trace formula comparison

statement: Proof of Theorem 4.1 combines Lefschetz fixed-point formula, Selberg trace formula and an explicit description of $\mathcal N_D(\mathbb F_q)$ analogous to Deuring's results on elliptic curves over F_p.
role: core comparison of two trace formulas

statement: For each eigenvalue \lambda of the p-adic endomorphism \alpha, with W_\lambda the generalized eigenspace and r_\lambda=\dim W_\lambda/\sum_i D_i W_\lambda, the function satisfies \prod_{\lambda}(1-\lambda t)^{r_\lambda}-type identity: the quotient of characteristic series \chi_F(t)/\chi_F(qt) is a polynomial expressed through the eigenvalues (the formula is garbled in the OCR; statement paraphrased).
hypotheses: Section 4 setting: F built from a hypersurface; \alpha=\psi\circ F acting on a space L(b) with the stated range of b

statement: \chi_F(t)/\chi_F(qt)-type product equals \det(I-t\alpha) on the quotient \mathfrak{B}=L(b)/\sum_i D_i L(b), provided b>1/(p-1) (OCR-garbled exact formulation).
The map \alpha induced on \mathfrak{B} is a nonsingular endomorphism, hence the relevant factor (called f^{(1+n)} in the OCR) is a polynomial of degree d^n-type (exact degree formula not legible).
hypotheses: Nonsingularity of all coordinate sections S_A (relaxed in 4c)

statement: \det(I-t\alpha)=\prod_{A}\det(I-t\alpha_A), the product over all subsets A of S={1,...,n+1}, where \alpha_A is the restriction to the image of the subspace of power series divisible by X_1...X_{n+1}-type monomials.

If (2,p,d)=1 then P_S(t)=\det(I-t\alpha_S) and \deg P_S = \frac{(d-1)^{n+1}+(-1)^{n+1}(d-1)}{d} (as read from the OCR; the paper's own formula is d^{-1}\{(d-1)^{n+1}+(-1)^{n+1}(d-1)\}). This is the polynomiality and degree part of the Weil conjectures for the hypersurface.
hypotheses: Section 4c removes the nonsingularity of all coordinate sections via an argument of Igusa

statement: If F has coefficients in a finite extension K_0 of Q_p and \lambda^{-1} is a zero of order \mu of \chi_F, then the kernel in L(b) of (I-\lambda^{-1}... \alpha)^\nu has dimension at least \mu, with \mu independent elements in L(b)\cap K_0(\lambda)[[X]].
hypotheses: coefficients of F in a finite extension of Q_p

statement: A p-adic spectral theory for \alpha on L': Thm 2.3 bounds the kernel dimension of (I-\lambda\alpha)^\mu by the multiplicity of \lambda^{-1} as a zero of \chi_F; Thm 2.4 says for s\ge s_\lambda the generalized eigenspace stabilizes, lies in L(b), and has dimension equal to the zero multiplicity; Thm 2.5 gives a surjectivity statement (I-\lambda\alpha)(K[[X]]\cap L(b)) for algebraic \lambda.
hypotheses: F has coefficients in a finite extension of Q_p

statement: A Koszul-type exactness criterion: if a certain complex of spaces of power series is exact in degree r=0 for all pairs of subsets 0\ne A\subset B of S, then it is exact for all r.
hypotheses: exactness at r=0 for all pairs A,B

statement: Function-theoretic properties of one-variable p-adic power series over the completion \Omega of the algebraic closure of Q_p: factorization of entire series by Newton polygon and a Hurwitz-type theorem on limits of zero sets (OCR garbled; statement paraphrased).
role: Supplies the zero-counting tools used to relate \chi_F zeros to eigenvalues of \alpha.

statement: L(1/(p-1)) = V + \sum_i D_i L(1/(p-1)) for the relevant finite-dimensional V; so \alpha maps onto \mathfrak{B} in Theorem 4.3.
role: Surjectivity giving nonsingularity of \alpha on the quotient.

statement: For b>1/(p-1), V\cap\sum_i D_i L(b)=\{0\}.
role: Makes the quotient space finite-dimensional with the correct dimension.

statement: Dimension and independence statements for the action of differential operators D_i on L(b) and on subspace L_S(b) of power series divisible by X_1...X_{n+1}; Lemma 3.19 computes dimensions via a polynomial identity.
role: Used to prove Theorem 4.4 by identifying the A-parts of the quotient with images of L_A.

statement: \alpha\circ D_i = q\,D_i\circ\alpha-type commutation relations (OCR garbled) for the differential operators D_i.
role: Explains the pairing of zeros \lambda^{-1} and (q\lambda)^{-1} in the characteristic series and is the reason to pass to the quotient by \sum D_i L(b).

statement: For \sigma\ge1+\varepsilon, |\zeta(\sigma+it)| lies between finite positive limits (Euler product); via the functional equation \zeta(s)=\ldots\zeta(1-s), for \sigma\le-\varepsilon one has |\zeta(\sigma+it)|=h\,|t|^{1/2-\sigma}; in the critical strip |\zeta(\sigma+it)| grows less than a finite power of |t| (Euler summation, eq. (4)); and (Mellin 1900) \zeta'/\zeta-type expressions (6) are bounded on the lines \sigma=1 and \sigma=0 up to log factors: |\zeta(1+it)|=O(\log|t|), |\zeta(it)|=O(|t|^{1/2}\log|t|) (Landau 1908 refinements are cited in a footnote).

Let f(s) be single-valued analytic in the half-strip-type domain \sigma_1\le\sigma\le\sigma_2, |t|\ge t_0, regular at all finite points of the domain, with |f|\le M on the two boundary lines (or bounded by a finite quantity), and with |f(s)|\le C|t|^{\mu}-type growth (condition 3: |f(s)|\,/\,|t|^{\alpha} bounded for some finite \alpha). Then the bound proved on the boundary persists in the interior. (Particular case of the Phragmen-Lindelof theorem established with Phragmen in a recent Acta Math. memoir; proof sketched via e^{\varepsilon i s}f(s) and the maximum principle.)

For every \varepsilon>0, \zeta(\sigma+it)=O\big(|t|^{(1-\sigma)/2+\varepsilon}\big)... precisely, with h as defined in the paper, the expression \frac{|\zeta(\sigma+it)|}{|t|^{\,(1-\sigma)/2}\ldots} stays below a finite limit in the domain 0\le\sigma\le1, |t|\ge t_1>1. (Printed form: 'L'expression ... 1-sigma ... reste au-dessous d'une limite finie dans le domaine 0<=sigma<=1, |t|>=t_1>1.' It is the convexity bound \mu(\sigma)\le(1-\sigma)/2 on [0,1] with logarithmic factors; exact power is a reconstruction since the display is garbled.) Note: the paper states it with greater precision than previous bounds (Mellin's \zeta(\sigma+it)=O(t^{(1-\sigma)/2+\ldots}), Landau 1908).

As an application of the lemma (section 4, via F(s)=s^{?}\ldots\sin(\pi s/2)\Gamma(1-s)\,\ldots and f(s)=\zeta(s)/F(s)): the growth exponent \mu(\sigma) (for suitable definition) is nonincreasing/convex, and the expression |\zeta(\sigma+it)|\,|t|^{-\,a} does not tend to zero for any \sigma in the critical strip for a below a computed value; in particular, for every \varepsilon>0 and \sigma in the stated interval \ |\zeta(\sigma+it)|\,/\,t^{\,\ldots-\varepsilon} does not tend to 0 (Section 5, p. 349-350, 'limite inferieure de la croissance').

label_in_source: End of Part I (pp. 354-356), the question
statement: Does |\zeta(1/2+it)|\,|t|^{-\varepsilon} stay bounded for every \varepsilon>0, or more generally does |\zeta(\sigma+it)| stay bounded for every \sigma>1/2? If so one obtains 'relatively simple results' about the growth of \zeta: \mu(\sigma)=0 for \sigma\ge1/2 (hence \mu(\sigma)=1/2-\sigma for \sigma\le 0 and 1/2-\sigma/... piecewise linear by convexity and functional equation). Also stated (p. 355): if one admits with Riemann that \zeta(s)\neq0 for \sigma>1/2 then \zeta(\sigma+it) for \sigma>1/2 stays below a finite limit up to \sigma'-\varepsilon, i.e. RH \Rightarrow Lindelof hypothesis (the printed claim: 'on peut demontrer que ... reste inferieur a une limite finie' for \sigma\ge\sigma'+\varepsilon). This is the first statement of the Lindelof hypothesis.
hypotheses: RH (Riemann: zeta(s)!=0 for Re s>1/2) for the implication
Lindelof hypothesis is posed as a question, not proved

statement: Phragmen-Lindelof principle on a half-strip: if f is regular and of finite order in \sigma_1\le\sigma\le\sigma_2,|t|\ge t_0 and satisfies |f|<M on the boundary lines then |f|<M in the interior (with the e^{\varepsilon i s} trick).
role: Engine for convexity bounds and for the function mu(sigma) log-convex.

label_in_source: Section 6 lemma (harmonic function in an angle)
statement: Let u(x,y) be harmonic, finite and continuous in the domain \sigma_0\le\sigma, a sector of opening < pi, regular inside, with r^{-\nu}|u| bounded for \nu<\lambda. If \limsup_{r\to\infty}u\le0 on each bounding ray then u<\varepsilon in the interior sector for r large; and dually for liminf. (Proved by conformal mapping onto a disc and Poisson's integral/Schwarz.)
role: Tool for the lower bound argument: show that if |zeta| were too small on one boundary, one gets a contradiction on the real axis, so that mu is a convex function and the growth limits are sharp.

statement: The expressions \zeta(1+it)\,/\,\log|t| and \zeta(it)/(|t|^{1/2}\log|t|)-type are bounded for |t|\ge t_0 (Mellin, Acta Soc. Sc. Fennicae 29, 1900, pp. 4-49; refined by Landau, Bull. SMF 33 (1905)).
role: Boundary values on sigma=0,1 for the Phragmen-Lindelof lemma.

statement: Schmidt proved \psi(x)-x=\Omega_\pm(\sqrt x) (i.e. there is K>0 with |\ldots|>K\sqrt x for arbitrarily large x, eq. (1)); under RH \psi(x)-x=O(\sqrt x\log^2 x) and \pi(x)-\mathrm{Li}(x)=O(\sqrt x\log x) (eq. (2), as printed: O(sqrt(x) log x)). Littlewood announces: \psi(x)-x=\Omega_\pm\big(\sqrt x\,\log\log\log x\big), \pi(x)-\mathrm{Li}(x)=\Omega_\pm\big(\sqrt x\log\log\log x/\log x\big), i.e. for arbitrarily large x each difference exceeds K\sqrt x\log\log\log x (resp. divided by \log x) in absolute value (eq. (3): K\,\sqrt{x}\,\log\log\log x/\log x). He proves the statement assuming RH ('Dans le cas contraire, on sait deja plus').
hypotheses: RH assumed in the proof (if RH fails, a stronger Omega result is already known from zero off the line)

statement: Let \eta_0>0 and S(\ldots)=\sum (\ldots) an almost periodic-type sum over zeros \rho=1/2+i\gamma_n; there exist values of the variable such that the real part of the sum exceeds a given bound with positive density, so that the extremal oscillation of the trigonometric series \sum\ldots can be forced to be at least \log\log\log-large by a quantitative Kronecker choice of arguments. (Statement is largely garbled in OCR: it asserts existence of values for which two inequalities hold simultaneously.)

For a positive number n_0, a sum S(\ldots)=\sum_n(\ldots)\ldots of the oscillating form \sum e^{i\gamma_n\log x}/\rho_n weighted over zeta zeros takes, for suitable arguments, values larger than a stated positive quantity; the first inequality is proved by an elementary argument using formula (9) as \varepsilon\to0, the second by a Kronecker-theorem argument (as used by H. Bohr in Dirichlet series).
role: Core of the Omega result: converts the zero sum into an oscillating series with arbitrary phases; log log log x is the growth of the 'effective number of independent oscillations' obtainable from the zeros.

statement: Using Kronecker's theorem (as exploited by Bohr), choose T such that \|\gamma_n T/2\pi\|<\ldots simultaneously for finitely many n (x_n=\|x-[x]\| distance to nearest integer); with (6),(7) a curve C: \sigma=\xi(n) (positive, continuous, decreasing) exists on which the Dirichlet-type function is bounded uniformly in the domain 0\le\xi\le\xi(n); a contradiction with the lemma of section 2 (extended to this domain) shows the assumed one-sided bound is false.
role: Argument by contradiction giving the sign changes and the size sqrt(x) log log log x.

statement: Let $L>0$, $D$ a real distribution on $[0,L]$ and $\tilde D$ the associated even distribution on $[-L,L]$. Assume the quadratic form with Schwartz kernel $\tilde D(x-y)$ defines a lower-bounded selfadjoint operator on $L^2([-L/2,L/2])$ whose minimum of the spectrum is a simple isolated eigenvalue with even eigenfunction $\eta$. Then all zeros of the entire function $\hat\eta(z)$ lie on the real line.
hypotheses: minimum of spectrum simple, isolated, even eigenfunction
location: Sec. 6.1, p. 26 (proof only sketched: trigonometric basis, finite matrices, Hurwitz)

statement: For the Weil quadratic form restricted to functions supported in $[1,13]$ (primes <= 13, prime powers 2,3,4,5,7,8,9,11,13), the Mellin transform of the minimizer eta has zeros on the critical line (provided the minimum eigenvalue is simple and even, footnote 12), and its first 50 zeros differ from the true zeta zeros by amounts listed from $2.60179\times10^{-55}$ (first zero) up to $0.0209081$ and $0.00212727$ (last listed); computed with trigonometric truncation N=100.
conditional_on: simplicity and evenness of lowest eigenvalue (footnote 12)
convergence as x to infinity (explicitly not proved)

label_in_source: Proposed proof strategy (end of Sec. 5, Sec. 6.6)
statement: If the minimal eigenvectors eta_x (recentered theta_x(u)=eta_x(x^{1/2}u)) converge in a suitable sense so that their Fourier transforms converge uniformly on compacts to Riemann's Xi, then by Hurwitz and Thm 6.1 all zeros of Xi are real, i.e. RH. Remaining steps: show the lowest eigenvalue of Q_{W_lambda} is simple with even eigenvector, and that k_lambda approximates theta_x well enough.
conditional_on: simplicity of smallest eigenvalue of Q_W,lambda
uniform convergence of Fourier transforms on compacts

statement: $\Xi(t)=\int_0^\infty k(u)u^{it}d^*u$ with $k=E(h)$, $E(f)(u)=u^{1/2}\sum_{n\ge1}f(nu)$, and $h$ (up to scalar) the unique linear combination of Hermite functions $h_0,h_4$ (eigenfunctions of $H=-\partial^2+4\pi^2u^2$) with vanishing integral; explicitly $h(u)=\frac{\pi}{2}(2\pi u^2-3)e^{-\pi u^2}$ up to normalization.

Eigenvalues $
u_n(\lambda)$ of $P_\lambda\hat P_\lambda P_\lambda$ on $L^2([-\lambda,\lambda])^{ev}$ are simple, $1>
u_0>
u_1>\dots>0$, eigenfunctions the even prolate spheroidal functions $h_{2n,\lambda}$ of the prolate operator $PW_\lambda=-\partial_x(\lambda^2-x^2)\partial_x+(2\pi\lambda x)^2$; $1-\chi_0,1-\chi_2	o0$ exponentially in $x=\lambda^2$; $1-\chi_2\sim rac{2^{14}}{3}\sqrt{2\pi}\,e^{-4\pi e^{L}+9L/2}$-type double-exponential decay in $L=2\log\lambda$ (cited from [47] Thm 1).

The Fourier transform of $k_\lambda=E(h_\lambda)|_{[\lambda^{-1},\lambda]}$ (with $h_\lambda$ the combination of $h_{0,\lambda},h_{4,\lambda}$ with vanishing integral) converges as $\lambda\to\infty$ to Riemann's $\Xi$ uniformly on closed substrips of the strip of width 1; on $\Im z=\alpha$, $\alpha\in(-1/2,1/2)$, the difference is $\le c\lambda^{-1/2-\alpha}(1-2\alpha)^{-1}$.

Let $g\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R_+^*)$ be supported in $[2^{-1/2},2^{1/2}]$ with Fourier transform vanishing at $i/2$ and $0$. Then $W_\infty(g*g^*)\ge \mathrm{Tr}(\vartheta(g)S\vartheta(g)^*)$, $S$ the projection on the Sonin space.

Assuming RH, with $D$ self-adjoint with spectrum the ordinates of the zeros, as $t\to0$: $\mathrm{Tr}\exp(-tD^2)\sim\frac{2\log(1/t)}{4\sqrt\pi\sqrt t}-\frac{\log4\pi+\gamma/2}{\sqrt2\sqrt\pi\sqrt t}+2\exp(t/4)+\sum a_nt^{n/2}$, $a_0=-1/4$, with $a_{2k-1},a_{2k}$ given by Bernoulli and Euler numbers; the series is divergent (factorial growth).

The sheaf $\mathcal O\rtimes\mathbb G_m$ on Spec Z has sections $S(\mathbb A_S)\rtimes\mathbb Z_S^\times$ over $S^c$, generic stalk $S(\mathbb A_{\mathbb Q})\rtimes\mathbb Q^\times$, global sections $S(\mathbb R)\rtimes\{\pm1\}$. Prolate operator $PW_\lambda$ restricted to Sonin space has discrete negative spectrum $\nu_k$ with $2\sqrt{-\nu_k}$ (for $\lambda=\sqrt2$) matching the UV asymptotics of $\rho-1/2$ (Connes-Moscovici [27]).

label_in_source: Weil positivity (Sec. 4.1) as used in Sec. 6.4
statement: RH iff the Weil quadratic form Q_W is positive on test functions; restricted form Q_{W_lambda} on support [1/lambda,lambda] has smallest eigenvalue epsilon(lambda)>0 under RH, tending to 0 exponentially in mu=lambda^2 (numerics of [25]).
role: framing of the minimization

statement: $E(\hat f)(x)=E(f)(x^{-1})$ for $f\in S_0^{ev}$ (f(0)=\hat f(0)=0); hence E(f) with f supported in [-lambda,lambda] and \hat f supported there too would lie in the radical of Q_{W_lambda}; obstruction is $P_\lambda\cap\hat P_\lambda=\{0\}$ but the projections nearly intersect.
role: conceptual justification of the near-radical ansatz k_lambda

statement: $W_\infty(f)=\log(TW)f(1)+\mathrm{Trace}(\vartheta(f)(1-P_T-\hat P_W))$ (archimedean trace formula), extended by (22) to include primes in S.
role: bridge between explicit formulas and time/band limiting

statement: Any fact that translates directly to a statement about characteristic polynomials of random unitary matrices (for which the RH analogue is true) cannot be used as evidence against RH; any fact from numerical computation of zeta, other than an actual counterexample, cannot be used as evidence against RH.

Lehmer pairs (e.g. gap <0.054 at zero 6709) do not suggest RH is 'barely true' in any meaningful sense because nearest-neighbour spacings of CUE eigenvalues are supported on all of $(0,\infty)$; RH is barely true anyway in other senses ($Z(t)\pm\delta$ has nonreal zeros; $\Lambda\ge0$ by Rodgers-Tao so $\Lambda=0$ is the only value consistent with RH).

The 'tightly packed spikes' picture of Z(t) with growing oscillation (Ivic) is forced even without RH since a positive proportion of zeros lie on the line and carrier waves are expected; appearance is a matter of axis scaling.

For smooth $f$ on a neighbourhood of $[-a,a]$ with distinct zeros $x_0,\dots,x_n$ in the interval: $\sum_{k=1}^r\Psi_{2k-1}(x,a)f^{(2k-1)}(a)-\sum_{k=1}^r\Psi_{2k-1}(x,-a)f^{(2k-1)}(-a)=\int_{-a}^a\Psi_{2r-1}(x,t)f^{(2r)}(t)\,dt$, where $\Psi_\ell$ is given by Bernoulli polynomials and weights $\mu_k(x)$ with $\sum_k\mu_k=0$.

For $T$ sufficiently large, $\delta>1/2$, $a=o(T/\theta'(T))$ and $\delta\theta'(T)\le2K\le2\theta'(T)^2$: $|Z^{(2K)}(t)|\le2\zeta(1/2+\delta)\theta'(T)^{2K}$ for $t\in[T-a,T+a]$, where $\theta'(t)\sim\frac12\log\frac t{2\pi}$.

label_in_source: Analysis of Blanc's argument (Sec. 12.3) and Reason 3 conclusion
statement: Blanc's contradiction from a large zero gap needs the left side of (12.1) large and the right side small. Farmer shows (using Table 12.5 from Bober-Hiary data) that the left side need not be large (Psi_1(x,a) tiny, or cancellation from other terms), and that Theorem 12.6 fails for characteristic polynomials only because the number of derivatives needed for 'cosine as universal attractor' is much larger there, so the argument evades Principle 12.1 yet is not shown to give a contradiction.

Ivic's conjecture $E_k=k/4$ for error terms in $\int_0^TZ^{2k}$ rests on the two data points $E_1=1/4,E_2=1/2$; any other formula (e.g. $E_k=3/4-2^{-k}$, which would imply LH) fits equally; $2k$-th moment asymptotic structure changes at $k=4$ (Conrey-Gonek), more affecting main terms than error terms.

A nontrivial linear combination of L-functions will not satisfy RH (Principle 13.1) and will have infinitely many zeros in $\sigma>1$ (Principle 13.2; theorem for Dirichlet L [Saias-Weingartner], automorphic L, and axiomatic settings). Deuring-Heilbronn function $F_{DH}$ (mod 5 character $\chi_{5,2}$) has first off-line zero near $0.8085+85.699i$ and infinitely many zeros with $\sigma>1$; Bombieri-Hejhal show 100% of zeros on the line for sums of L-functions with same functional equation under additional hypotheses.

Z(t) near t0 is governed by a slowly varying carrier wave (determined by local zero density fluctuations / primes, Principle 10.1), a local universal (CUE/GUE) factor and a global factor; Keating-Snaith law models Z(1/2+it) by characteristic polynomials; Theorem 9.8 (Backlund) LH iff $N(\sigma,T+1)-N(\sigma,T)=o_\sigma(\log T)$ for all $\sigma>1/2$.
LH holds iff $N(\sigma,T+1)-N(\sigma,T)=o_\sigma(\log T)$ for every fixed $\sigma>1/2$.
role: imported result used for the LH versus self-reciprocal polynomials comparison

statement: For a self-reciprocal polynomial Z(z) of degree N in polar form with D=z d/dz, $D^{2K}Z(z)\to$ (N/2)^{2K}z^{-N/2}(z^N+1+o(1)) as K to infinity: roots of D^{2K}Z approach Nth roots of -1 (equal spacing).
role: explains 'cosine is a universal attractor' and why Blanc's bound needs a specific K range

statement: For $z^{-N/2}(z+1)^N$ and $\kappa N$ D-derivatives with $\kappa<1$ a high-multiplicity zero at z=-1 remains; even N derivatives leave $D^N$ large at z=1 (coefficient $N-\sqrt N$ argument).
role: shows the Blanc theorem analogue is false for unitary polynomials

statement: Z(t) is statistically indistinguishable from -Z(t); any finite sequence of normalized gaps occurs with positive proportion, so snapshots of Z are random-matrix-like.
role: foundation for Reason 2 refutation

statement: The function $\zeta(s)$ has infinitely many zeros on the line $\sigma=1/2$; equivalently Riemann's $\Xi(t)=\xi(1/2+it)$ (real for real $t$) has infinitely many real zeros. Proof by contradiction: if $\Xi(2t)$ kept a constant sign for $t>T>1$ one gets an impossible inequality.

From the Cahen-Mellin integral $e^{-y}=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{k-i\infty}^{k+i\infty}\Gamma(u)y^{-u}du$ ($\Re y>0,k>0$) one gets $1+\frac1{\pi i}\int_{k-i\infty}^{k+i\infty}\Gamma(u)y^{-u}\zeta(2u)du=1+2\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-n^2y}$ ($k>1/2$); moving to $\Re u=1/4$ and using $\Xi$: $1+\sqrt{\pi/y}-\frac2\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(\pi/y)^{1/4+ti}\frac{\Xi(2t)}{1/4+4t^2}dt=1+2\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-n^2y}$.

With $y=\pi e^{i\alpha}$, $|\alpha|<\pi/2$, $q=e^{i\pi\tau}=e^{-y}$ and $F(q)=1+2\sum q^{n^2}=\vartheta_3(0,\tau)$: $\int_0^\infty\frac{(e^{\alpha t}+e^{-\alpha t})\Xi(2t)}{1/4+4t^2}dt=\pi\cos\tfrac14\alpha-\tfrac12\pi e^{\frac14 i\alpha}F(q)$, and differentiating $2p$ times in $\alpha$: $\int_0^\infty\frac{(e^{\alpha t}+e^{-\alpha t})t^{2p}\Xi(2t)}{1/4+4t^2}dt=\frac{(-1)^p\pi}{4^{2p}}\cos\tfrac14\alpha-\big(\tfrac{d}{d\alpha}\big)^{2p}[\tfrac12\pi e^{\frac14 i\alpha}F(q)]$.

As $\alpha\to\pi/2$ (so $q\to-1$ along a path tangent to the ray $\arg q=\pi$), every $(d/dy)^{2p}F(q)=2\sum n^{4p}q^{n^2}\to0$, for each $p$; justified by Bohr-M. Riesz summability of the Dirichlet series $1^{-s}+0+0-4^{-s}+\dots$ representing $(1-2^{1-2s})\zeta(2s)$, which is entire of finite order in half-planes and has value $(1-2^{1-2s})\zeta(2s)=0$ at negative integers $s$ (hence Cesaro-summable to 0).

Hence as $\alpha\to\pi/2$: $\int_0^\infty\frac{(e^{\pi t/2}+e^{-\pi t/2})t^{2p}\Xi(2t)}{1/4+4t^2}dt=\frac{(-1)^p\pi}{4^{2p}}\cos\frac{\pi}{8}$ (if $\Xi(2t)$ has constant sign for $t>T$, the tail $\int_T^\infty$ has that sign).
hypotheses: Xi(2t) of fixed sign for t>T>1 (the assumption to be contradicted)

statement: For odd $p$: $\int_T^\infty<-\int_0^T<KT^{2p}$ with $K$ independent of $p$, while if $\Xi(2t)>\delta>0$ on $(2T,2T+1)$ then $\int_T^\infty>\delta K_1(2T)^{2p}$; so $\delta K_1 2^{2p}<K$ for all odd $p$, absurd for large $p$.
hypotheses: fixed sign of Xi(2t) beyond T (and a lower bound delta on a unit interval, implicitly by continuity/non-vanishing assumption)

label_in_source: Cahen-Mellin integral (cited from Cahen, Ann. ENS 1894, p.99; Mellin, Acta Soc. Fenn. 20 (1895))
statement: $e^{-y}=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{k-i\infty}^{k+i\infty}\Gamma(u)y^{-u}du$ for $\Re y>0$, $k>0$.
role: Converts the theta series into an integral of Xi against a kernel, linking zeros of Xi to theta-function behaviour.

statement: A Dirichlet series with an entire continuation of finite order in half-planes is summable by Cesaro means of sufficiently high order everywhere, with the value given by the continuation.
role: Gives that all derivatives $(d/dy)^{2p}F(q)\to0$ as $q\to-1$, so the right side of (3) tends to the explicit constant in (4).

kind: theorem about a random model (almost sure), transferred to primes only as a suggestion
statement: In the urn model with independent draws, with probability $1$: $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{P_{n+1}-P_n}{(\log P_n)^2}=1$. The argument: events $E_m=\{$black balls from all $U_{m+\nu}$, $1\le\nu\le c(\log m)^2\}$ have probability $\varepsilon_m$ with $A m^{-c}<\varepsilon_m<B m^{-c}$; Borel-Cantelli gives finitely many for $c>1$, and infinitely many for $c<1$ by using independent blocks $m_{r+1}=m_r+[c(\log m_r)^2]+1$.

There are absolute constants $\lambda>0$, $\tau_0$ such that for $\tau>\tau_0$ and $\tau\log^2\tau\,e^{-\tau}<\sigma<1/\tau^2$, with $\Delta=\frac{\lambda\sigma\tau}{\tau+\log\sigma}$: $\pi(e^{\tau+\Delta})-\pi(e^{\tau-\Delta})>\frac{\sigma e^\tau}{\tau}\bigl(1-3\,\Re F(s)\bigr)$, where $s=\sigma+i\tau$ and $F(s)=\sum_{\gamma>0}e^{-(\gamma-i\beta)s}$ is the sum over zeros $\rho=\beta+i\gamma$ in the upper half plane.

For some $\delta>0$ and all large $x$ there is a prime in $(x,x+cx^{1-\delta}]$, hence $p_{n+1}-p_n=O(p_n^{1-\delta})$. Needs the unproved (detailed proof not given here) estimate (26) for $\sigma=e^{-\delta\tau}$; a footnote says Tchudakoff's 1936 zero-density claim lets $\delta$ be any number $<1/4$.

If RH holds, then $p_{n+1}-p_n=O(\sqrt{p_n}\,\log p_n)$. In fact for large $x$ there is a prime in $(x,x+5\lambda\sqrt x\log x]$. Proof: under RH $|F(s)|\le e^{-\tau/2}\sum_{\gamma>0}e^{-\gamma\sigma}$, and by $N(T)=\frac{T}{2\pi}(\log\frac T{2\pi}-1)+O(\log T)$ one gets $\sum_{\gamma>0}e^{-\gamma\sigma}\sim\frac1{2\pi\sigma}\log\frac1\sigma$. Choose $\sigma=\tau e^{-\tau/2}$, so $\Re F\to 1/(4\pi)<1/3$ and Lemma 3 applies.
location: pp. 36-37, Theorem I (first proved in Cramér 1919, [4])

statement: Assume RH. Let $\sigma(\tau)\downarrow0$ with $0<\sigma<1$. Then there is an absolute $K$ such that for all $t>m$, $\int_t^{t+1}|F(\sigma(t)+i\tau)|^2d\tau<K e^{-t}\frac{\sigma(t)}{\sigma^2(t+1)}\log^2\frac1{\sigma(t+1)}$. For $\sigma=e^{-c\tau}$ with $1/2<c<1$ this is $<Kt^2e^{-(1-c)t}$, i.e. $\Re F$ is small on average.

Assume RH. For $h(x)=x^\alpha\log^\beta x$ let $S_{\alpha,\beta}(x)=\sum_{p_n\le x,\ p_{n+1}-p_n>h(p_n)}(p_{n+1}-p_n)$ and $N_{\alpha,\beta}(x)=\#\{p_n\le x: p_{n+1}-p_n>h(p_n)\}$. Then (39a) $S_{\alpha,\beta}(x)=O\!\bigl(\frac{x\log^3x}{h\log h}\bigr)$ for $0\le\alpha<1/2,\beta\ge0$ and for $\alpha=1/2,0\le\beta\le1$; (39b) $S_{1/2,\beta}(x)=O(1)$ for $\beta>1$; (40a) $N_{\alpha,\beta}(x)=O\!\bigl(\frac{x\log^3x}{h^2\log h}\bigr)$ for $0\le\alpha<1/2,\beta\ge0$; (40b) $N_{1/2,\beta}(x)=O(\log^{3-2\beta}x)$ for $0\le\beta\le1$; (40c) $N_{1/2,\beta}(x)=O(1)$ for $\beta>1$. In particular, with $h=\log^3x$: $\sum_{p_n\le x,\ p_{n+1}-p_n>\log^3p_n}(p_{n+1}-p_n)=O(x/\log\log x)=o(x)$.

kind: theorem; part b) second half conditional on RH
statement: a) $\sum_n\frac{p_{n+1}-p_n}{p_n\log^\lambda p_n}$ diverges for $\lambda\le1$ and converges for $\lambda>1$. b) $\sum_n\frac{(p_{n+1}-p_n)^2}{p_n\log^\lambda p_n}$ diverges for $\lambda\le2$; and, if RH holds, converges for $\lambda>4$. Proof of convergence: split by $p_{n+1}-p_n\le\log^\beta p_n$ or $>$, with $2<\beta<3$ and Theorem II estimates (55)-(57), giving $\sum_{x<p_n\le2x}(p_{n+1}-p_n)^2<Kx\log^{2\beta-1}x$, hence $\sum_{p_n\le x}(p_{n+1}-p_n)^2=O(x\log^{3+\varepsilon}x)$.
conditional_on: Riemann hypothesis (for convergence of (54) when lambda>4)

statement: $\Re H(s)=\pi+O(1/\tau)$ uniformly in $D=\{0<\sigma\le1,\tau>1\}$, where $H(s)=2\pi F(s)+G(s)$ and $G(s)=\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\Lambda(n)}n\bigl(\frac1{s-i\log n}+\frac1{i\log n}\bigr)$. Unconditional.
role: Relates the zero sum F to the prime sum G through an explicit formula from Cramer 1919/[3] (formula (13) p. 114 there), so that the prime sum is dominated by n near e^tau.

statement: For positive $a,b$ there is $C(a,b)$ with $\sum_{x<n\le x+h}\frac{\Lambda(n)}n<C\frac{h\log x}{x\log h}$ for $x>2,h>2,a\log x<h<bx$. Unconditional, by a Brun-Titchmarsh-type sieve bound for short intervals (via Brun and Hardy-Littlewood estimates cited as [1],[7]).
role: Controls the contribution of tails S_2,S_3,S_4 in the proof of Lemma 3.

statement: As above: $\pi(e^{\tau+\Delta})-\pi(e^{\tau-\Delta})>\frac{\sigma e^\tau}{\tau}(1-3\Re F)$ for $\tau\log^2\tau\,e^{-\tau}<\sigma<\tau^{-2}$.
role: Fundamental lemma: lower bound for primes in an interval of width approximately 2 Delta in log scale, in terms of the zero sum F. All of Theorems I, II and the Hoheisel proof follow from it.
location: p. 31, proof pp. 31-35, split sums S_1..S_4, Poisson-type kernel sigma/(sigma^2+(tau-log n)^2)

statement: Mean-square bound for F on vertical unit segments under RH, as above.
role: Replaces a pointwise bound of Re F by an average bound; essential for Theorem II (exceptional gaps are rare).
location: p. 37-39, proof via $|f(\sigma+i\tau)|^2\le\sigma\int|\Phi(v,\tau)|^2e^{-v\sigma}dv$ and the Fejer-type kernel $g(x)=2-|x|$ and $N(T)$ estimate

statement: Let $H,K>0$ be constants, $s=\sigma+it$ with $-H\le\sigma\le H$, and $x>K$, $y>K$, $2\pi xy=|t|$. (i) $\zeta(s)=\sum_{n<x}n^{-s}+\chi(s)\sum_{n<y}n^{s-1}+R$ with $\chi(s)=2(2\pi)^{s-1}\sin(\tfrac12 s\pi)\Gamma(1-s)$ and $R=O(x^{-\sigma})+O(y^{\sigma-1}|t|^{1/2-\sigma})$. (ii) If in addition $x\ge y$, $R=O\big(x^{1-\sigma}/(|t|^{1/2}+x\,\mathfrak S(y))\big)$ where $\mathfrak S(y)$ is the distance from $y$ to the nearest integer. (iii) If $x\le y$, $R=O\big(|t|^{1/2-\sigma}y^{\sigma}/(|t|^{1/2}+y\,\mathfrak S(x))\big)$. The O-constants depend only on $H,K$.

Uniformly for $0\le\sigma\le H$: $\zeta(s)=\sum_{n<x}n^{-s}+\chi'\sum_{n<y}n^{s-1}+O(x^{-\sigma})+O(|t|^{1/2-\sigma}y^{\sigma-1})$ with $\chi'=(|t|/2\pi e)^{-it}(|t|/2\pi)^{1/2-\sigma}e^{\frac14\pi i\,\mathrm{sgn}\,t}$. In particular for $\sigma=1/2$, $x=y=\sqrt{|t|/2\pi}$: $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)=\sum_{n<x}n^{-1/2-it}+(|t|/2\pi e)^{-it}e^{\frac14\pi i\,\mathrm{sgn}\,t}\sum_{n<x}n^{-1/2+it}+O(|t|^{-1/4})$; hence $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)=O(t^{1/4})$.

(i) For $1/2<\sigma<1$, as $T\to\infty$: $\frac1{2T}\int_{-T}^{T}|\zeta(\sigma+it)|^4dt\sim\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{[d(n)]^2}{n^{2\sigma}}=\frac{[\zeta(2\sigma)]^4}{\zeta(4\sigma)}$. (ii) $\int_{-T}^{T}|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|^4dt=O[T(\log T)^4]$. (iii) $\int_{2}^{T}|\zeta(\sigma+it)|^4dt=O[T(\log T)^4]$ uniformly for $1/2\le\sigma\le2$, $T>2$.

$\int_{-T}^{T}|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|^2dt\sim2T\log T$ as $T\to\infty$ (already due to Hardy-Littlewood 1917, Acta Math. 41, pp. 151-156; new short proof from Theorem C with $x=t/(2\pi\sqrt{\log t})$, $y=\sqrt{\log t}$).
location: Section 3.1, p. 59-61 (proof of the case $\int|Z|^2\sim T\log T$)

statement: $\int_{-T}^{T}|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|^4dt=O(T\log^4T)$, described as 'a further stage in the direction of Lindelof's hypothesis' $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)=O(|t|^\epsilon)$ (which would follow from $\int|\zeta|^{2p}=O(T^{1+\epsilon})$ for every p).

Let $d_k(n)$ be the number of representations of $n$ as an ordered product of $k$ factors and $\Delta_k(x)=\sum_{n\le x}d_k(n)-x P_{k-1}(\log x)$ the Piltz error term. For every integer $k\ge4$ and $\epsilon>0$: $\Delta_k(x)=O(x^{\frac{k-2}{k}+\epsilon})$, i.e. $\alpha_k\le\frac{k-2}{k}$, where $\alpha_k$ is the infimum of exponents $\theta$ with $\Delta_k(x)=O(x^{\theta+\epsilon})$.

The fourth-power bound (4.21) $\int_{-T}^T|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|^4dt=O(T^{1+\epsilon})$ yields $\alpha_k\le (k-2)/k$ for $k>3$ [(4.22)]. A further improvement $\alpha_k\le (k-1)/(k+2)$ for $k>3$ [(4.23)] would follow from the (then unpublished, 'lies very deep') estimate (4.24) $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)=O(t^{1/6+\epsilon})$. statement: Fix real $\lambda>0$, $r\ge0$, $q\in\mathbb N$, an $N\times N$ matrix $(c_{kl})$ with $(c_{kl})^2=I$, and integers $b_1,\dots,b_N$. Such systems correspond bijectively to systems $g_k(\tau)$, $\tau=x+iy$, with: (1) $(\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2+\frac{r^2+1/4}{y^2})g_k=0$, regular in $y>0$; (2) $g_k=O(y^{\kappa_1})$ as $y\to\infty$, $O(y^{-\kappa_2})$ as $y\to0$ uniformly in $x$; (3) $g_k(\tau+\lambda/q)=e^{2\pi i b_k/q}g_k(\tau)$; (4) $g_k(-1/\tau)=\sum_l c_{kl}g_l(\tau)$. The correspondence is via Mellin transform and Fourier expansion $g_k=u_k(y)+\sum_{n\neq0}a_n^{(k)}y^{1/2}K_{ir}(2\pi|n|y/\lambda)e^{2\pi i n x/\lambda}$ with $u_k$ explicit in (16).

statement: If \lambda>2, then for every k>0, \gamma=\pm1 there exist infinitely many linearly independent functions \varphi of signature \{\lambda,k,\gamma\}.

For \lambda=2 the number of linearly independent \varphi of signature \{2,k,\gamma\} is finite: for \gamma=1 it equals \lfloor k/4\rfloor+1; for \gamma=-1 it equals \lfloor (k-2)/4\rfloor+1 if k\ge2 and 0 otherwise. In particular \{2,1/2,1\} has only \zeta(2s) (up to constant) and \{2,1,1\} only the zeta function of \mathbb{Q}(i).

For 0<\lambda<2 solutions of signature \{\lambda,k,\gamma\} exist only if \lambda=2\cos(\pi/q), k=\frac{4K}{q-2}+1-\gamma with positive integers q\ge3, K. The number of solutions is \le \lfloor (K+(\gamma-1)/2)/q\rfloor+1, and the number regular at s=k is exactly \lfloor (K+(\gamma-1)/2)/q\rfloor. For 0<\lambda<1 there are none. Consequently the zeta function of \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3}) is determined up to constant by signature \{\sqrt3,1,1\}.

Signature \{1,k,\gamma\} (modular group G(1), q=3) has no solutions unless k is even and \gamma=(-1)^{k/2}; then the number of independent solutions is \lfloor k/12\rfloor if k\equiv2 \pmod{12}, and 1+\lfloor k/12\rfloor otherwise (dimension of modular forms of weight k, via f(\tau) with group G(\lambda)).

For L-series modulo q / zeta functions of \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-q}) the system (3)+(IV) has only finitely many linearly independent solution systems (the group \mathfrak{M} is finite, isomorphic to a binary modular group mod q or 2q); for integer k\ge2 the number of solution systems explicitly involves the class number of \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-q}); for prime D, zeta functions with Grossencharacters are singled out as eigen-objects (characteristic roots) of a matrix given by the data. statement: A real sequence $(\alpha_k)_{k\ge0}$ is a Faktorenfolge of the first kind if for every polynomial $\sum_{k\le n}a_kx^k$ with only real roots, $\sum_{k\le n}\alpha_ka_kx^k$ has only real roots. A sequence $(\beta_k)$ is of the second kind (as written in the paper's terminology: sequences such that the transformation preserves real-rootedness) when it does so for polynomials with all real roots of the same sign (positive-root-only class, the paper states it with the weaker hypothesis on the input and conclusion 'no imaginary root'). Constants count as real-rooted polynomials. Examples attributed to Laguerre: $1,q,q^4,q^9,\dots$ ($|q|\le1$ in the paper's notation for the squares-exponent sequence) are of the first kind; $\cos\vartheta,\cos(\vartheta+\delta),\cos(\vartheta+2\delta),\dots$ are of the second kind. First kind implies second kind; the converse fails (e.g. the cosine sequence unless $\delta$ is a multiple of $\pi$).

A real sequence $(\alpha_k)_{k\ge0}$ is a Faktorenfolge of the first kind iff for every $n\ge1$ the polynomial $\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk\alpha_kx^k$ has only real roots, all of the same sign. [Paper's formulation: 'dann und nur dann ... wenn alle Gleichungen (11.) $\alpha_0+\binom n1\alpha_1x+\dots+\alpha_nx^n=0$ lauter reelle Wurzeln von gleichem Vorzeichen besitzen'.]
A real sequence $(\beta_k)$ is a Faktorenfolge of the second kind iff for all $n$ the polynomial $\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk\beta_kx^k$ has only real roots (eq. 12).

Case $\lambda_0=0$ handled in (30).
role: Exact identity from which analytic continuation follows by Mellin-Barnes/contour integration in $\xi$.

statement: Multiplying (29) by $\frac{1}{2\pi i}(-\xi)^{-s}$ and integrating over a keyhole contour around the positive real axis gives $\sum\phi_m^2\lambda_m^{-s}=\frac{\sin\pi s}{\pi}\int\frac{M_n(\xi,P)-\gamma_n(P,P;-\xi)}{\xi^s}d\xi+(\text{entire})$, regular for $\Re s>N/2-n-2$ by the bound on $\gamma_n$; the explicit integral of $M_n$ yields the displayed poles and the zeros at non-positive integers.
role: Converts the resolvent identity into analytic continuation (Mellin transform of the resolvent).

statement: For squarefree $D\in\mathbb F_p[t]$, $Z_D(s)=\sum_{\mathfrak a}|N\mathfrak a|^{-s}$ converges absolutely for $\Re s>1$ with Euler product over prime ideals (split primes contribute $(1-|P|^{-s})^{-2}$, inert $(1-|P|^{-2s})^{-1}$, ramified $(1-|P|^{-s})^{-1}$) and satisfies a functional equation $s\leftrightarrow1-s$ (Eq. 8 and Section 21 Eqs 4-6 for real fields) relating $Z_D(1-s)$ to $Z_D(s)$ via an explicit factor in $p$ and $|D|$.
location: Part II, Sections 17, 21 (exact constants not reliably legible in OCR)

statement: $Z_D(s)$ has period $2\pi i/\log p$; its only poles are simple poles at $s=1+2\pi ik/\log p$; $Z_D$ has no zeros on $\Re s=1$ (Hadamard-de la Vallee Poussin argument via the Euler product logarithmic derivative; points $1+2\pi ik/\log p$ handled via the field $K(\sqrt{gD})$).

No zeros in $\Re s<0$. On $\Re s=0$: for $\deg D$ odd none; for $\deg D$ even only simple zeros at trivial points (imaginary field: $s=\pi ik/\log p$ type; real field: $s=2\pi ik/\log p$ type, including $s=0$). All other nontrivial zeros lie in a strip $0<1-\theta\le\Re s\le\theta<1$ symmetric about $\Re s=1/2$ and the real axis, $\theta=\sup\Re$ of the zeros.

For imaginary fields with $n=\deg D\ge3$, $Z_D$ is a polynomial in $p^{-s}$ (times a fixed factor) with coefficients $\sigma_
u$; with $ eta_

u-1)$ for $n$ even imaginary (Eqs 3-5 of Sec. 24); for real fields an analogous formula involving the regulator $R$.

RH ($\Re\rho=1/2$, i.e. $|\beta_\nu|=\sqrt p$) is verified case by case: about forty fields computed (introduction); Section 23 derives it for small $n$ (cubic discriminants via the table of class numbers, and 'ebenso' $n=5$ except for cases left to computation). The general proof is stated to be open, with difficulties 'of similar type as for Riemann's zeta' but clearer since the objects are essentially polynomials.

Assuming RH for all quadratic function fields: for imaginary fields with $n\ge3$, $(\sqrt p-1)^{n-1}\le h\le(\sqrt p+1)^{n-1}$ ($n$ odd) and $2(\sqrt p-1)^{n-2}\le h\le2(\sqrt p+1)^{n-2}$ ($n$ even) (Eqs 10-11, exponents as legible in OCR). Consequences: (1) for all $p,n$ only finitely many fields of prescribed class number; class number 1 only for $p=3$ (probably one field); (2) only finitely many fields with one-class genera, and only for $p=3,5,7$.
hypotheses: RH for all quadratic function fields

statement: For a character $\chi$ modulo $\mathfrak K$, $L(s,\chi)$ has no zero on $\Re s=1$; combined with Kornblum's regularity of $L$ for non-principal $\chi$ this sharpens Kornblum's theorem on infinitely many prime functions in arithmetic progressions (precise quantitative form not read).
Finiteness of the class number for imaginary quadratic function fields.
role: Basic finiteness input.

statement: Count of ambiguous classes; genus relation $h/f=2^{s-1}$ with $s$ the number of prime factors of $D$.
role: Bounds classes per genus in Section 24.

statement: Continued fractions of quadratic irrationals in $K((1/t))$; finiteness of class number for real fields; unit group, fundamental unit and regulator.
role: Real-field arithmetic for the class number formula.

statement: Quadratic reciprocity law in $\mathbb F_p[t]$ and generalization.
role: Decomposition of primes in $K(\sqrt D)$.

statement: Euler product with local factors for split/inert/ramified primes; $Z(s)$ expressed through the zeta function of $\mathbb F_p[t]$ and an L-factor.
